articles.title: Can’t hear your TV? These soundbars are the instant audio upgrade you need
articles.summary: These soundbars and speaker systems from Sonos, Samsung and JBL are an instant upgrade to your home entertainment system. Here’s what you should know before buying one.
articles.body: You may be wondering why you would ever need to buy a soundbar. If you’ve bought a great TV, you’ll expect to have good audio in the mix. But for most TVs, the audio you’re getting is a huge downgrade compared to what an external speaker can accomplish. That’s partially because of the slim nature of today’s flatscreen TVs. You may have noticed TV actors seem to mumble their dialogue or car crashes in an action movie are less explosive than the sound of your kettle, it’s probably because your TV speakers aren’t up to the task. I’m here to tell you that better audio is possible with a soundbar and speaker system. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. The best soundbars and speakers My top picks come from a mix of popular and NBC Selected staff-tested brands like Sonos, Sony, JBL and Roku. Staff-pick Former NBC Selected reporter Harry Rabinowitz has used this soundbar for over two years. It has a compact design that fits his smaller 48-inch TV, and it seamlessly connects with HDMI eARC and Wi-Fi. “It’s small and simple, but it’s drastically improved my TV-watching experience with its crystal clear sound,” says Rabinowitz. It can sync with other Sonos speakers over Wi-Fi to play music and other media in your space. Best budget standalone The Roku Streambar SE packs both a Roku streaming device and a soundbar into one, making it a neat solution for those tired of juggling various remotes and cables in their home entertainment setup. This entry-level model starts at $99, but is often discounted, and should offer a noticeable upgrade to average TV audio. It also replaces your television’ interface with a user-friendly and customizable Roku TV platform. Best budget with subwoofer You don’t need to spend thousands to get a multi-unit system, as you can see with the Sony HT-S400. This budget setup throws in both a basic soundbar and a wireless subwoofer, which allows you to space out the audio kit in a manner to your liking. It also has the heft needed to make bass frequencies audible. ARC support provides two-way device communication when connecting to your TV over HDMI, meaning that your TV speaker remote can control your TV and vice versa. Best mid-range This two-part sound system is a great pick for everyday audio listeners, with a handful of smart features you won’t get in cheaper models. For one, there’s Dolby Atmos support, with the 5.1 channel system to properly recreate its immersive audio design. But you’ll also get MultiBeam, which helps to direct the sound sideways instead of simply forward, allowing for a soundscape that travels across the room. Support for 4K Dolby Vision passthrough means you can even connect the speaker to a games console and transfer its signal to the television. If you’re short on ports anyone with a selection of Alexa speakers can link them up with the JBL Bar for multi-room audio. Best premium Samsung’s Q Series is a great place to look for a new TV speaker, especially if you’re sporting one of Samsung’s OLED or QLED TVs. But even if you don’t have a Samsung TV, the Q800F is a great choice for the price, packing in an impressive 5.1.2 channel system that includes an external subwoofer and Dolby Atmos audio support. Better yet, it’s easy to add other subwoofers if you ever want to unleash a real surround sound system. Best standalone soundbar With a 9.1.4 sound system, the Sonos Arc Ultra is one of the most impressive all-in-one soundbars you can get. Sonos has a reputation for high quality audio in my experience, whether you’re blasting through an action movie or drawing out the instrumental soundtrack on a thoughtful documentary. All of this is aided by Dolby Atmos and Dolby TrueHD support. Just know it’s pricey and doesn’t come with a subwoofer, though you can add a Sonos subwoofer separately for a bassier experience. How I picked the best soundbars I’ve worked as a gadget tester and home entertainment reporter for most of the past decade, with plenty of hands-on experience with soundbars, surround sound systems and TV audio. I have hands-on experience with a number of the models in this guide, and the industry knowledge needed to parse what’s worthwhile or good. When selecting these recommendations, I drew on the advice of multiple sources from the audio hardware industry — cited further down in this guide — and kept the below criteria in mind: Price: TV speakers can be a tricky proposition, given it’s easy to spend as much on one as you would the television itself. I focused on offering a range of options for different budgets while considering how extensive a multi-channel system should be for that price.Immersive audio: Dolby Atmos, DTS:X and Sony 360 Reality Audio are all immersive audio formats. Each format helps sound designers better cater to the intricacies of the multi-channel audio systems in consumers’ homes. I looked specifically for models that supported these formats and were able to create virtual surround sound even without multiple separate pieces of hardware. Bass output: The main thing lacking from TV audio is usually bass and low-frequency response, as flatscreen TV designs don’t easily fit hefty subwoofers. I made sure to include models with impactful bass or dedicated subwoofers included in the purchase. How to shop for the best soundbars and speakers Choosing the right speaker for you will depend on a host of factors, from your personal hardware budget and TV tastes to the size and scale of the room your TV is in. To that end, I spoke with two home entertainment experts to get a better sense of what a prospective speaker shopper should look for. TV speaker audio channels When shopping around for sound systems, you may see a series of numbers that look confusing, such as 2.1, 3.1.2, 5.1 and 7.1. These are all multi-channel speakers, indicating the number of channels and how they are arranged. In 3.1.2, you’ll get three center channels, one subwoofer for bass output and two height-oriented channels. In a 2.1 system, that’s only two center channels and one subwoofer, without height-oriented audio. TVs tend to come with a two-channel stereo system (so, 2.0 in this terminology). A good 3.1.2 audio system allows for a meaningful upgrade that gives your audio a sense of direction and scale, though a proper 5.1.2 or 7.1.4 system will make your movie nights feel truly cinematic. Consider your space John Couling, Senior Vice President of Entertainment at Dolby Laboratories, says to make sure your multi-channel system is appropriate for the size of your space: “A higher audio channel configuration (like 5.1.2) will work great in a larger room, like the living room in a single family home, as it will provide a more encompassing sound field needed for the space. Alternatively, a more compact soundbar (say a 3.1.2 or 2.1 system), which features less audio channels, may work better and sound equally impressive in smaller rooms.” TV speaker manufacturers will often try to sell you on ‘virtual’ surround sound, despite not having the speakers to really create that effect — essentially using an algorithm to upscale audio and a little directional trickery to make you think you’re experiencing surround sound. Couling praises these “advancements in psychoacoustic processing” — psychoacoustic being the study of sound perception in the human body. It won’t have the full effect of a physical surround sound system roaring around you, but can offer something like the immersion of high-end systems at a more affordable price point. As Couling says, “This means immersive audio capabilities can be found in sound bars at really compelling prices. This is important because it means great sound and immersive audio is now accessible to a wider audience.” Pay attention to bass Ole Moltsen, a product manager at audio brand Bang & Olufsen, recommends looking for speakers with “bass capability”, as this is usually what’s lacking from TV speakers, but admits that “it can be quite difficult for people to compare technical specifications between brands and products”, which makes product reviews or buying guides like these usually the best place to start. For Couling, the real feature to look for is “immersive audio capabilities”, but agrees that extra bass is a major reason to upgrade to a soundbar: “If you want extra bass, make sure the soundbar comes with a sub or consider adding one to your purchase if it doesn’t. Many will also come with rear speakers that you can pair with your soundbar, which are a great addition.” Meet our tech experts At NBC Selected, we work with experts who have specialized knowledge and authority based on relevant training and/or experience. We also take steps to ensure all expert advice and recommendations are made independently and without undisclosed financial conflicts of interest. John Couling is the senior vice president of entertainment at Dolby Laboratories, is an industry specialist and former Dolby applications engineer now overseeing the company’s global partnerships strategy.Ole Moltsen is a product manager at Bang & Olufsen, a premium Danish consumer electronics brand. Why trust NBC Selected? I am a freelance technology reporter with extensive experience covering streaming services, reviewing TVs and testing user interfaces for a host of consumer gadgets. I previously worked as the News & Features Editor at TechRadar and now freelance for NBC Selected, CNET and The Independent. articles.title: Incêndio em Itaquaquecetuba atinge loja de som no Cidade Kemel | G1
articles.standfirst: Fogo foi controlado horas depois. Ocorrência foi registrada por volta das 13h e quatro viaturas do corpo de bombeiros foram enviadas ao local. Ninguém se feriu.
articles.summary: Incêndio em Itaquaquecetuba atinge loja de som no Cidade Kemel; bombeiros controlaram as chamas e a Defesa Civil avalia se a estrutura do imóvel foi comprometida.
articles.body:
Incêndio no limite entre Itaquaquecetuba e Itaim Paulista — Foto: Imagens cedidas / Theo Leite

Um incêndio atingiu uma loja de aparelhos de som e acessórios automotivos na tarde desta terça-feira (3), no bairro Cidade Kemel, em Itaquaquecetuba . O estabelecimento fica no limite com o distrito de Itaim Paulista, na Zona Leste de São Paulo.

Segundo o Corpo de Bombeiros, a ocorrência foi registrada por volta das 13h e quatro viaturas foram enviadas ao local. Ninguém se feriu.

A Defesa Civil de Itaquaquecetuba informou que uma equipe do órgão também auxiliou no atendimento à ocorrência. O fogo foi controlado horas depois.

As medidas adotadas incluem uma avaliação técnica do imóvel para verificar se o incêndio comprometeu a estrutura.

O órgão disse ainda que permanecia no local para acompanhar a ocorrência e adotar medidas de segurança e prevenção de novos riscos.

articles.title: Orçamento do Amazonas cai e prevê R$ 37,2 bilhões para 2027 | G1
articles.standfirst: Proposta, enviada à Assembleia Legislativa do Estado pelo governador Roberto Cidade, estabelece como os recursos públicos serão distribuídos e utilizados pelo governo estadual no próximo ano. Texto será analisado e votado.
articles.summary: O orçamento do Amazonas para 2027 prevê R$ 37,2 bilhões, com redução justificada pelo fim de receitas extraordinárias e foco em áreas como saúde e educação.
articles.body:
Proposta de Lei Orçamentária Anual (LOA) foi enviado para deputados do Amazonas nesta terça-feira (3). — Foto: Matheus Rodrigues/Aleam

O Governo do Amazonas encaminhou à Assembleia Legislativa do Estado (Aleam) a proposta de orçamento para 2027, primeiro ano da gestão de Omar Aziz (PSD). O projeto prevê R$ 37,2 bilhões em receitas e despesas, valor R$ 768 milhões menor que o orçamento aprovado para 2026 .

A proposta estabelece como os recursos públicos serão distribuídos e utilizados pelo governo estadual no próximo ano.

Na mensagem enviada aos deputados, o governador Roberto Cidade (União Brasil) justificou a redução com dois fatores. O primeiro é que, em 2026, o estado recebeu R$ 780 milhões em uma arrecadação extraordinária, que não deve se repetir em 2027.

O segundo é a previsão de descontos de R$ 772 milhões relacionados a créditos do Imposto sobre Circulação de Mercadorias e Serviços (ICMS).

Cidade também afirmou que a redução na previsão de recursos "não reflete uma deterioração econômica".

A Secretaria de Estado da Fazenda (Sefaz-AM) concentra a maior previsão orçamentária, com R$ 8,64 bilhões. O valor inclui recursos destinados ao cumprimento de obrigações financeiras do estado.

As áreas de educação e saúde aparecem na sequência, com previsões de R$ 5,65 bilhões e R$ 4,74 bilhões, respectivamente.

Para a segurança pública, estão previstos R$ 3,32 bilhões. Já a infraestrutura deve receber R$ 167 milhões, enquanto a área de meio ambiente tem previsão de R$ 89,3 milhões.

O projeto também estabelece os valores destinados aos demais Poderes e órgãos estaduais:

Tribunal de Justiça do Amazonas (TJAM): R$ 1,654 bilhão ;

Assembleia Legislativa do Amazonas (Aleam): R$ 706 milhões ;

Ministério Público do Amazonas (MPAM): R$ 569 milhões ;

Tribunal de Contas do Estado (TCE-AM): R$ 503 milhões ;

Defensoria Pública do Estado (DPE-AM): R$ 238 milhões .

A proposta será analisada inicialmente pela Comissão de Assuntos Econômicos da Assembleia Legislativa, que deverá designar um relator e estabelecer os prazos para a apresentação de emendas pelos deputados.

Em seguida, o projeto passará pela Comissão de Constituição e Justiça (CCJ). Depois dessas etapas, o texto será levado à votação em plenário.

articles.title: Bienal de Arquitetura e Urbanismo em Brasília: confira programação | G1
articles.standfirst: Evento gratuito vai até 6 de novembro, com o lema 'Cuidar da vida'. Bienal reunirá grandes nomes da arquitetura e urbanismo para debater sobre os novos desafios urbanos.
articles.summary: A Bienal de Arquitetura e Urbanismo em Brasília oferece debates, mostras de cinema e visitas guiadas gratuitas para discutir o futuro das cidades até 6 de novembro.
articles.body:
Começa nesta terça-feira (3) a 14ª Bienal Ibero-Americana de Arquitetura e Urbanismo (BIAU) em Brasília, com programação até a sexta-feira (6).

Com o lema " Cuidar da vida ", o evento reflete sobre os desafios das cidades e dos territórios. As inscrições são gratuitas para a sequência de debates, premiações e atividades culturais.

Nesta edição, grandes nomes arquitetura e urbanismos participar: Angelo Bucci, Fernando Pérez Oyarzún, David Barragán, Marta Maccaglia, Inês Lobo, Solano Benítez, Loreta Castro e Marcelo Rosenbaum. — Foto: foto: Joana França/ Divulgação SESI Lab

Nesta edição, a bienal reunirá profissionais da arquitetura, do urbanismo, do pensamento e da cultura em torno de quatro eixos (água, vegetação, habitação e comunidades) para explorar as dinâmicas da relação entre a arquitetura e as condições ambientais, sociais e culturais.

A programação da bienal está espalhada por diferentes locais da capital do modernismo brasileiro, entre debates, mostras de filmes, conferências temáticas, lançamentos de livros e visitas guiadas pela cidade ( confira abaixo a programação completa ).

➡️ O registro e a inscrição nas atividades pode ser feito de forma presencial.

A abertura da Bienal foi na tarde desta terça, no auditório do SESI Lab – espaço que recebe parte das atividades ao longo da semana.

O evento mobiliza também áreas do Teatro Nacional, da Universidade de Brasília, do Cine Brasília, da Galeria Index e da Embaixada de Portugal.

Dentre as atividades espalhadas pela cidade, a Bienal preparou três visitas guiadas a locais de referência da arquitetura e do urbanismo de Brasília . As datas e locais estão disponíveis na programação completa e no site do evento.

Além das rotas turísticas, o evento terá sessões de cinema com a curadoria da arquiteta, urbanista e pesquisadora Liz Sandoval. As sessões serão no Cine Brasília, espaço histórico da capital federal.

As sessões foram realizadas como extensão dos debates sobre a ligação da arquitetura, urbanismo, patrimônio, participação social com a transformação dos territórios.

Os dois filmes documentários apresentados serão dividos em duas sessões.

Na primeira, serão exibidos "Brasília", do diretor Antonio Carlos da Fontoura e "Crônicas de uma cidade inventada", da diretora Luísa Caetano.

Na segunda, será exibido o longa "Hacer mucho con poco (Do more with less)" dos diretores Katerina Kliwadenko e Mario Novas.

articles.title: Aeroportos: Garanhuns e Serra Talhada entram em plano de concessão | G1
articles.standfirst: Medida abre caminho para que empresas privadas assumam a administração dos aeroportos.
articles.summary: Os aeroportos de Garanhuns e Serra Talhada foram incluídos no Programa Nacional de Desestatização para viabilizar melhorias na infraestrutura e nos serviços.
articles.body:
Aeroporto de Garanhuns — Foto: Thomas Ravelly

Os aeroportos de Garanhuns , no Agreste de Pernambuco, e de Serra Talhada , no Sertão, foram incluídos em um programa federal que prevê a concessão de terminais regionais à iniciativa privada. A medida foi oficializada pelo presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), por meio do Decreto nº 13.142/2026, publicado no Diário Oficial da União (DOU) nesta terça-feira (3).

Com a decisão, os dois equipamentos passam a integrar o Programa de Parcerias de Investimentos (PPI) e o Programa Nacional de Desestatização (PND). A inclusão tem como objetivo viabilizar a concessão dos aeroportos a empresas privadas.

Na prática, a concessão permite que uma empresa assuma a administração dos aeroportos por um período determinado. Em contrapartida, a concessionária deve cumprir compromissos relacionados a investimentos na infraestrutura e na melhoria dos serviços.

A medida não significa a venda dos aeroportos. Na modalidade de concessão, os terminais continuam sendo públicos, mas a administração fica sob responsabilidade da empresa vencedora do processo.

articles.title: Ciara Mageean: Funeral of Olympian takes place
articles.summary: The former European champion and two-time Olympic runner had been diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer.
articles.body:
Olympian Ciara Mageean has been described as a "truly remarkable, immensely talented and inspirational human being" in a tribute read out at her funeral.

Hundreds of people have paid their respects to the runner at her funeral on Tuesday.

The former European champion and two-time Olympic runner died on Sunday after she was diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer.

Among those in attendance at the funeral in Portaferry, County Down, were Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill, as well as fellow Olympian Rhys McClenaghan and 1972 gold medallist Lady Mary Peters.

Mageean's funeral cortege was given a guard of honour by Portaferry GAC and her former school, Assumption Grammar in Ballynahinch.

Her death comes less than three weeks after her marriage to her long-term partner Thomas Moran.

Mourners began arriving at around midday for the 2:00 GMT requiem Mass at St Patrick's Church.

Family, friends and those wishing to pay their respects followed the funeral cortege the short distance along the Ballyphilip Road from Mageean's family home to the church.

Others in attendance included representatives for Irish President Catherine Connolly and the Irish Government, Social Democratic and Labour Party leader Claire Hanna, GAA President Jarlath Burns and former boxer Paddy Barnes.

The Mass booklet included an image of Mageean's greatest achievement on the track, the moment she crossed the line at the 2024 European Championships.

In his homily, Father Martin Kelly, who knew Mageean from her childhood, spoke of her accomplishments, her love for her husband and the joy and pride she had brought to her hometown.

Kelly recalled visiting her in hospice shortly before her death, when she suggested they go for a walk.

Despite her illness, Mageean noticed he was struggling and offered to link arms with him.

"On the way down, she knew I was struggling and she said, 'Let me link you'," he told mourners.

"One of my happiest moments and memories is that of Ciara Mageean linking my arm as we walked back to her room."

The athlete represented Ireland at the 2016 and 2020 Olympics and won gold in the 1500m at the European Athletics Championships in Rome in 2024.

She also represented Northern Ireland at the Commonwealth Games, winning silver in Birmingham in 2022.

Noticing blood in your poo - which may appear black or dark red in the toilet bowl - can be a sign of bowel cancer.

If there is no other obvious cause for the bleeding, such as piles, the NHS recommends that you ask for an appointment with your GP .

The NHS also advises a check-up if you notice changes in your regular toilet habits, such as having to poo more often, or a pattern of diarrhoea or constipation.

Abdominal pain or lumps, stomach bloating and unexplained weight loss are also among symptoms which should lead to a bowel cancer test.

Bowel cancer can also cause anaemia, the features of which include extreme tiredness and shortness of breath.

The earlier bowel cancer is detected, the easier it is to treat.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Zelenskyy hopes Abu Dhabi talks will open path to Putin meeting
articles.summary: Ukrainian president meets German chancellor in Berlin, who says Russia is yet to engage seriously in peace efforts.
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he hopes upcoming United States-mediated talks with Russia in Abu Dhabi will lead to a three-way meeting of leaders that includes Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Speaking in Berlin on Tuesday alongside German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Zelenskyy said the adviser-level talks, set for November 10 and 11 , were part of a broader diplomatic push to end the war.

“We are counting on the fact that work in this format and our other diplomatic steps will open the way to a trilateral format at the level of leaders,” Zelenskyy told reporters.

Asked about the Abu Dhabi talks, Merz said it was “important that Russia finally and seriously engages in negotiations about a ceasefire and a subsequent peace agreement”.

“I do not see that happening so far,” the chancellor said.

Zelenskyy’s visit to Berlin was not announced in advance for security reasons.

On landing, he said on X that diplomatic coordination, strengthening air defences and supporting Ukraine’s energy sector would top the agenda.

US special envoy Steve Witkoff announced the new round of talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US on Monday. He said the discussions would focus on “post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace”.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed that a Russian delegation would attend, led as before by former Culture Minister Vladimir Medinsky, the state news agency TASS reported.

The build-up to next week’s talks follows one of the most notable displays of cooperation between the warring sides since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Last week, human rights ombudsmen from Russia and Ukraine oversaw a local ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky to evacuate residents and deliver aid, in a mission brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump.

Putin and Zelenskyy have had no direct contact since the invasion, and their representatives have held only a handful of rounds of talks.

Al Jazeera’s Dominic Kane, reporting from Berlin, said there was a clear sense from Zelenskyy and Merz that the Abu Dhabi meeting “is a step forward, and there was an element of positivity about it”.

He said one journalist raised an important issue, saying “Europe and Ukraine are supposedly in lockstep with each other”, before asking, “why then are the Europeans not going to be in Abu Dhabi in those talks?”

“There was not much of a reply there, but it’s clearly an issue, a thorny issue, perhaps, certainly for the Europeans,” Kane said.

European governments have insisted on being involved in the negotiations but are unlikely to be at the table in Abu Dhabi.

Instead, US envoys are due to meet representatives from Germany, France, the United Kingdom, NATO and the European Union in Brussels this week to discuss security guarantees for Ukraine and Europe’s post-war security architecture.

Zelenskyy has said Ukraine needs an additional 70 billion euros ($77.5bn) from European countries next year.

Kane said successive German governments had pledged their full support to Ukraine, financing its efforts to fend off Russian attacks and supplying weapons and ammunition.

But he said Merz knows that “the financial aspect of helping Ukraine has become a real issue, given that the economy here and in other European countries is particularly threatened right now”.

“The cost of living in this country for many voters has become a serious issue,” Kane said.

He added that parties opposed to funding Ukraine, including the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the left-wing Die Linke, were “prospering in the polls and in elections”.

Several summits are planned before year-end

US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Putin may hold three-way talks on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on November 18 and 19 .

Around the same time, the so-called Coalition of the Willing, a group of about 35 countries backing Ukraine, is due to meet in Berlin.

The Group of 20 (G20) summit follows in Florida from December 13 to 15 , where it remains unclear whether Putin will attend for the first time since the invasion.

articles.title: Poole Museum fundraises for masthead sculpture homage to carers
articles.summary: The sculpture by Jason Wilsher-Mills was created for the artist's exhibition at Poole Museum.
articles.body:
A museum is appealing for help to keep a colourful masthead sculpture, created as a homage to carers.

The work is part of a major exhibition at Poole Museum in Dorset, by artist Jason Wilsher-Mills, and was inspired by the museum's collections.

Wilsher-Mills, who is disabled, said the sculpture was a nod to "the unsung heroes of our society... who deserve our recognition and lasting gratitude".

Poole Museum, which is celebrating its first birthday following a major revamp, has already secured nearly £10,000 of funding and is appealing for a further £10,000 to buy the piece.

Ahead of the free exhibition, which runs until 3 January, Wilsher-Mills said: "I've always been drawn to coastal places, and Poole really captured my imagination.

"The figureheads in the museum stayed with me and inspired new work for this show."

Wilsher-Mills, who hails from Yorkshire, suffered a life‑changing illness during his childhood which left him paralysed for a year when he learned to paint using a brush held in his mouth.

He first came to Dorset in 1992 as an art student and, in 2025, he was made a MBE for Services to Art and Disability.

He said: "This modern masthead is dedicated to carers - the unsung heroes of our society.

"As a disabled person, the spotlight often falls on me, but it's carers who deserve our recognition and lasting gratitude.

"The people who cared for me come up a lot in my art.

"There's a tapestry for my mum and dad, who cared for me when I was told by doctors I wouldn't make it to 16 - and here I am at 57.

"We can't do enough to thank and recognise what carers do."

Poole Museum said it had a "once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to permanently secure this iconic masthead sculpture".

It has so far secured £10,000 from the Arts Council England/V&A Purchase Grant Fund.

articles.title: Trump's planned 250-foot memorial arch near Arlington Cemetery could begin construction this week, but a federal judge has now ordered rapid court notifications and warned against work without proper approval
articles.summary: A giant arch planned for Washington’s Memorial Circle is moving closer to the construction stage, but the Donald Trump administration’s push to begin work
articles.body: A giant arch planned for Washington’s Memorial Circle is moving closer to the construction stage, but the Donald Trump administration’s push to begin work this week is now tangled in a fast-moving legal battle. The proposed 250-foot structure, envisioned as part memorial, tourist attraction and national-security facility, has drawn lawsuits from veterans, local governments and preservation advocates concerned about its scale, setting and impact on the landscape around Arlington National Cemetery, according to online reports.Court puts construction plans under close watchThe latest development came Monday, when US District Judge Tanya Chutkan imposed strict notification requirements on the administration as she weighs challenges to the project. According to AP News, officials must notify the court within an hour of any decision by the National Capital Planning Commission, the National Park Service or the Interior Department related to the arch. The order also requires the government to provide notice within 30 minutes of any activity connected to or preparing for construction.Chutkan further warned that beginning construction or demolition before the National Park Service issues its final authorization, or proceeding without the required 14-day notice, could violate earlier court orders, AP News reported. The deadlines matter because the administration has indicated that construction could begin as soon as November 5, following the anticipated planning commission decision.A massive structure near ArlingtonThe proposed memorial is considerably more elaborate than a conventional commemorative monument. According to AP News, the administration submitted a 106-page plan outlining a structure rising more than 12 stories and featuring a large bronze representation of Lady Liberty, complete with wings and a torch bearing an eternal flame.Plans include an observation deck offering views in both directions, an occupied roof and two mezzanines. The interior would contain offices, programme areas, staff facilities, elevators, staircases and a fire command centre. The development would also require significant changes to traffic patterns around Memorial Circle and surrounding roads.Why the administration wants itAs per CNN report, the arch was initially presented as a monument connected to the United States' 250th anniversary. The administration has subsequently placed greater emphasis on its potential national-security role.CNN reported that government lawyers have argued the site could accommodate military equipment, including drones and ammunition, while also functioning as a major tourist destination. Officials have also cited security concerns surrounding the president.That argument came under scrutiny during a court hearing, where Chutkan questioned how the structure's proposed security function would work alongside its expected public use. The administration has estimated that as many as 22,000 civilians could visit the site each day.Lawsuits are piling upThe project is facing challenges from multiple directions. According to CNN, three Vietnam veterans and an architectural historian have sued to stop the development, while Washington, DC, and Virginia have filed a separate case seeking emergency action. Arlington County has also challenged the project.The veterans argue that the arch could affect the character and solemnity of Arlington National Cemetery while disrupting a prominent visual corridor connecting the Lincoln Memorial and the cemetery.Chutkan is considering a preliminary injunction in the veterans' case. After the District of Columbia and Virginia filed their separate lawsuit, the cases were consolidated, creating a coordinated legal schedule that could determine whether construction proceeds.The timing is now crucialOne of the central issues before the court is whether challengers would have enough opportunity to seek judicial review if construction were allowed to start immediately after the planning commission approves the project. CNN reported that Chutkan questioned what would constitute final agency action if bulldozers had already begun digging. The concern is particularly relevant because the administration's own timeline could leave opponents with little time between final approvals and the start of construction.For now, the project remains caught between an administration determined to move ahead and a federal court demanding that every procedural step be followed. With a key planning decision approaching, the coming days could determine whether the proposed arch moves from plans on paper to construction at one of Washington's most consequential landscapes.Images Courtesy: Instagram and US Commission of Fine ArtsYou use AI every day. articles.title: Opposition party organiser killed before South Africa elections
articles.summary: Police are investigating the motive in murder of MKP coordinator as political killings rise during municipal elections.
articles.body:
An organiser from an opposition party has been killed in South Africa’s KwaZulu-Natal province, raising concerns about political violence before Wednesday’s local government elections.

⁠Senior police spokesman Robert Netshiunda said on Tuesday that a murder investigation had been opened after Lastborn Shazi – identified by the uMkhonto weSizwe Party (MKP) – was shot dead late on Monday at his home while on a Zoom call coordinating the party’s election campaign.

Police are investigating the motive, Netshiunda said.

South African police said last weekend that 20 murders involving political representatives, party members and supporters had been recorded during the municipal election period.

Last week, South African President ‌‌Cyril Ramaphosa ordered the deployment of more than 500 soldiers to KwaZulu-Natal to support police, who have ‌‌identified ‌‌more than 165 polling stations in the province as high-risk.

Voters on Wednesday will elect councillors, who will then choose mayors to oversee municipal services, including water, sanitation and rubbish collection.

Recent polls project the ⁠⁠MKP to emerge as the ⁠⁠largest party in the closely contested eThekwini metropolitan area – the economic hub of KwaZulu-Natal – and displace the governing African National ⁠⁠Congress (ANC) there.

Former President Jacob Zuma leads the MKP after ⁠⁠a bitter split with the ⁠⁠ANC in 2023. The party’s rise helped erode the ANC’s support in the 2024 national election.

The ANC lost its parliamentary majority in 2024 and formed a unity government with the Democratic Alliance (DA), the second-largest party, and smaller parties.

In the last municipal elections in 2021, the ANC lost control of several big cities. It governs others through coalitions.

articles.title: Keeping mortgage interest relief in Guernsey approved
articles.summary: Homeowners can get tax relief of £3,500 on the money spent on the interstate of a mortgage.
articles.body:
A move to keep tax relief on interest paid on mortgage payments has been approved.

Deputy Aidan Matthews, who brought the amendment to the Budget in Guernsey, said it was currently the "worst possible time" to consider phasing out the tax relief. It also meant that the phased withdrawal of the relief, which was agreed in 2015, would also stop, it was confirmed.

The relief allows homeowners to apply for tax relief on any interest paid on the mortgage of their principle residence of up to £3,500 a year.

Speaking against the move, Deputy Neil Inder said that, while the idea was right in isolation, if all amendments were approved, it would add "£20m to the budget".

Alderney representative Alex Snowdon said the timing of the amendment was "important".

He said: "There is a lot of Guernsey and Alderney people will be working two to three jobs that are really struggling to try and support the mortgage and their families.

"I think this sends a strong message that we are trying to do a little bit to try and help people who are going through a very difficult time.

"Some might say [these are] normal interest rates, but we've had money so cheap for so long that we are getting back to more difficult interest rates because house prices are going up so much people are borrowing so much more money."

Deputy Jayne Ozanne said in the debate that she was "very split" on the amendment because it was an "unfair advantage" to homeowners over renters.

"This will not solve the crisis of people leaving the island," she said.

"They can not afford to save for a deposit for a mortgage because they are paying such high rents," she said.

"Their monthly outgoings does not allow them to create the capital egg that they need to put a deposit down. This will not help that; it may help them once they've got a mortgage to decide to stay.

"I'm wrestling because I feel there is an inequality here... the average rent in the island is over £2,000 per month while the average mortgage, I believe, is £1,000.

"But two wrongs don't make a right. I recognise that families are feeling squeezed."

articles.title: After months lost at sea on a small boat, 5 people are rescued in the island nation of Kiribati
articles.summary: Five people, including two children, were rescued this week in the South Pacific island nation of Kiribati after three months drifting at sea in a 20-foot skiff, authorities said.
articles.body: MELBOURNE, Australia (AP) — Five people, including two children, were rescued this week in the South Pacific island nation of Kiribati after three months drifting at sea in a 20-foot skiff, authorities said. Another four remained missing. Villagers rescued the group Sunday off Fanning Island in Kiribati, the Australian Broadcasting Corp. reported, after they had drifted an estimated 5,400 kilometers (3,355 miles) east from the Federated States of Micronesia. The U.S. Coast Guard in Guam on Tuesday confirmed that the skiff with nine people aboard had been reported missing after it failed to return to Ruo Island in Micronesia on July 30. A 10-day search covering 85,700 square kilometers (33,000 square miles) followed without any sign of the missing boat or those aboard, it said. “Incredible and wonderful news these five folks were found and are receiving care,” the U.S. Coast Guard told The Associated Press in an email. “Our profound condolences to family and friends of those who did not arrive with them,” the email added. When asked by the AP what happened to the missing four, the U.S. Coast Guard said it was continuing to gather and confirm information and would reply as soon as possible. A lawmaker in Kiribati, Kaotitaake Rakoroa, told ABC the survivors were being cared for by a pastor on the island. Nursing officer Paukin Tororo told the ABC on Monday that all five were severely dehydrated and malnourished. All were put on intravenous drips and were showing signs of recovery. “They can give a smile face, they show the sign they want to eat,” she told the ABC. The survivors had yet to speak publicly about their ordeal and had requested privacy, the Australian broadcaster reported. The governor of Micronesia’s Chuuk state, Alexander Narruhn, issued a statement Sunday saying he had begun talks with the Kiribati government to bring the survivors home. “There were nine people aboard the boat that went missing. Thanks be to God for his love and mercy that five of the nine have been found,” Narruhn said through an interpreter. “We continue to pray for their four companions,” he added. Narruhn did not immediately respond to the AP’s request for comment. The nine had been making a one-hour crossing between the islands of Murilo and Ruo when they were caught in a storm, the ABC reported.

articles.title: Nicole Taylor of country music trio Taylor Red dies at 35
articles.summary: Her sisters and fellow group members Nika Taylor and Natalie Taylor, announced her death Monday in a social media post.
articles.body: Nicole Taylor, a member of the country music trio Taylor Red who was diagnosed with breast cancer four years ago, has died, according to her sisters and bandmates. She was 35. “We are shocked and heartbroken to announce the passing of our sister,” Nika Taylor and Natalie Taylor said in a social media post Monday. “She’s at peace and no longer suffering, so we’re thankful for that.” Originally from Mississippi, the identical triplets first began making music together in 2010 under the name Red Roots before renaming their band Taylor Red eight years later, eventually moving to Nashville, Tennessee. The country music trio became immensely popular online after their song “Country Money” went viral on social media in 2021. A year later, Nicole Taylor was diagnosed with stage 3 breast cancer. “I remember we were out in a public place, and she got a phone call from the nurse about her biopsy results,” Natalie Taylor said as part of a 10-minute social media video she did with Nika Taylor, opening up about their sister’s death. “And she was like, ‘You have cancer.’ I remember just breaking down in utter shock.” “If you know anybody with cancer, there’s so many MRIs, scans, treatments, appointments that you have to go through, and it’s very stressful,” Nika Taylor said in the video. Nicole Taylor’s cancer eventually progressed to stage 4, the sisters said. According to the band’s website, Nicole Taylor died Sept. 28 and her family held a private funeral service. “Nicole told us soon before she passed that she had peace, and we are really thankful for that,” Natalie Taylor said.

articles.title: Speeding Lamborghini driver jailed for killing friend in M62 crash
articles.summary: Humaira Batool, 26, is sentenced for causing for the death of 20-year-old Mohammed Shaan Hussain.
articles.body:
A driver who caused the death of her friend when she lost control of a rented Lamborghini and crashed into a motorway barrier has been jailed for 10 years.

Mohammed Shaan Hussain, 20, died when Humaira Batool crashed the £200,000 supercar on the M62, near Ripponden, in West Yorkshire, in December 2022, causing it to flip over and burst into flames.

During her trial, jurors heard Batool, 26, from Bradford, had been driving at speeds of up to 140mph (230km/h) in wet conditions shortly before the crash.

Passing sentence, Judge Ray Singh said Hussain died as a result of Batool's decision to drive the "powerful performance vehicle" at "eye-watering extreme speeds on a damp motorway in darkness".

The judge said: "This was not a momentary lapse of concentration. It was a conscious decision to drive at extraordinary speed in conditions that made such driving especially dangerous.

"You deliberately exposed your passenger, yourself and other road users to an obvious and grave risk of death or serious injury. Tragically, that risk materialised."

During the trial, the court heard Hussain, also from Bradford, had rented the vehicle and was driving to HMP Leeds with Batool to collect a friend.

The pair switched places en route and the car crashed off the carriageway within eight seconds of Batool taking the wheel.

In court, Batool tried to blame Hussain, saying he had "reached over" while she was driving and touched something, causing the car to surge, but this was rejected by the jury.

The judge said: "During the trial, various alternative explanations were advanced on your behalf, all of which were rejected – the possibility of mechanical failure, aquaplaning and your suggestion that, just prior to the collision, the controls of that vehicle had been tampered with by Shaan.

"The jury rejected those explanations. I do likewise.

"The sole cause of this collision was the manner of your driving."

Hussain died as a result of the injuries he sustained in the crash, while Batool suffered serious injuries, including burns to around 10% of her body and a shattered tibia.

Batool had been due to be sentenced on Monday but did not appear , with her barrister saying she had gone to A&E due to a flare-up of endometriosis.

Prosecutor Christopher Dunn claimed it was "clearly a ruse" and the judge issued a bench warrant for her arrest.

The judge told the court Hussain's death had been "tragic and entirely avoidable" and his life had been brought to a "sudden and horrific end".

"The suffering inherent in those final moments is difficult to overstate," he said.

"Death came not immediately upon impact but afterwards, whilst he remained unable to escape. That is a truly dreadful way for any human being to die."

In a victim statement read to the court, Hussain's mother Nasreen Akhtar said he was a "beloved son and cherished brother, a loyal friend and light in all our lives".

"Every day has been a struggle," she said.

"What has made this unbearable pain even worse is the impact of trying to mourn our son when we have had to listen to others try to tarnish him."

His brother Mohammed Souhail Hussain added: "Shaan was our older brother then. His is our older brother today and he will always be our older brother."

Batool was sentenced to 10 years in prison, disqualified for driving for 10 years and told she must pass an extended driving test.

Det Insp Paul Conroy said: "When any of us get behind the wheel we need to accept the responsibility of controlling a machine which can cause devastation if not handled responsibly.

"This especially applies when handling a car of the nature Batool drove that evening. Her driving put herself and anyone near her on the motorway at risk and it sadly resulted in the tragedy we have seen in this case."

articles.title: Former West Point cadet sued for drugging pregnant girlfriend, forcing abortion pills into her body
articles.summary: A former West Point cadet who has admitted to drugging his pregnant girlfriend and forcing an abortion on her in 2022 was sued by his former partner last week for assault and battery.
articles.body: A former West Point cadet who has admitted to drugging his pregnant girlfriend and forcing an abortion on her in 2022 was sued by his former partner last week for assault and battery. Caleb Suh pleaded guilty in June to assault resulting in substantial bodily injury to a dating partner, a federal crime in a maritime or territorial jurisdiction. Suh’s attorney declined to comment on the lawsuit when reached by NBC News. Suh is attending a graduate program at Columbia University as he awaits his January sentencing in U.S. District Court in Manhattan, according to the civil complaint. Columbia University declined to comment, citing federal privacy laws for students. The victim, identified in the lawsuit as Jane Doe, was a freshman and cadet at the West Point Academy when she was in a relationship with Suh, then a sophomore at West Point, according to the lawsuit. Jane Doe became pregnant with Suh’s child and said she would not get an abortion, according to the Oct. 28 lawsuit filed by Jane Doe’s attorneys, Russell Kornblith and Lily White. In spite of her decision, Suh “repeatedly demanded that Ms. Doe terminate the pregnancy” and threatened to kill himself if she didn’t, the suit said. Suh admitted to impersonating Jane Doe to obtain medication from an online pharmacy in her name. He forced her to drink what he said was a pregnancy protein shake, which was spiked with the depressant Xanax, that made her sick and caused her to fall asleep. As she faded in and out of consciousness, Suh forced abortion pills into her mouth and vagina, according to the lawsuit and his guilty plea. Jane Doe awoke in severe pain and was bleeding from her vagina. She was rushed to the hospital where she learned she had miscarried, the lawsuit says. The victim “has sustained in the past and will continue to sustain ... physical injury, monetary damages, pain and suffering, psychological and emotional distress, humiliation, and loss of career fulfillment,” the lawsuit alleges. Jane Doe is seeking unspecified monetary compensation and an acknowledgment that she was the victim of an assault and battery.

articles.title: Darfur survivors vow to tell story of those killed after Sudan camp attacks
articles.summary: Survivors of attacks on displacement camps in Darfur recall the lives they built, and violence that forced them to flee.
articles.body:
In a small house in Omdurman, Hassan Saber Jumaa, a senior administrator at the Zamzam displacement camp in Sudan, sat on a simple wooden chair. He scrolled through his phone, looking for any photograph he might have of Zamzam, which is near el-Fasher, the capital of North Darfur, and once sheltered hundreds of thousands.

He found nothing. Jumaa explained that his old phone was looted during last year’s attack by Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces on the camp. Pointing to the bare walls around him, Jumaa said that all he has left are his memories of the camp, and the people who once called it home.

Zamzam, established in 2004, was home to generations of people displaced by western Sudan’s Darfur war, which began in 2003 and continued for nearly two decades. Alongside Abu Shouk camp and al-Salam camp, Zamzam formed part of one of Darfur’s largest concentrations of displaced people.

Jumaa recalled a bustling community, with its market open every day, and children walking to school.

Zamzam continued as a refuge for civilians until Sudan’s current war, which began in 2023. The RSF, fighting the Sudanese Armed Forces and its allies, captured the camp in April 2025, after months of attacks. Famine had been confirmed in the camp in August 2024.

Mukhtar Musa, a survivor of the assault, watched the community he knew descend into starvation and violence. He said restrictions on the movement of goods had exhausted food supplies, leaving some residents with little choice but to eat animal feed and peanut shells.

Umm Kulthum Ali Saleh described the months before the final attack as the hardest of her life. The RSF siege on Zamzam stopped goods from entering. She searched for food every morning, and recalled seeing women cooking grass and mixing mud with flour to bake bread.

Saleh believes the blockade was not merely a military measure, but a deliberate way to weaken the camp’s residents in advance of the final offensive, and Zamzam’s fall.

On April 11, the RSF launched a three-day assault using cars, camels, and horses, burning straw homes and health facilities.

A United Nations Human Rights Office report documented at least 1,013 civilians killed, including 319 who were summarily executed in homes, markets, schools, clinics, and mosques. The report documented other abuses, including rape, gang rape, sexual slavery, and other forms of sexual violence, particularly targeting the Zaghawa community.

Musa was a witness to some of those mass killings, and said he saw RSF fighters kill civilians while chanting religious slogans. He described seeing bodies scattered around the main market and near schools, and said fighters continued pursuing civilians along roads leading out of the camp.

Saleh also recalled seeing bodies littering the roads, with only chickens, donkeys, and sheep wandering among the abandoned buildings.

The attack forced tens of thousands to flee Zamzam, with many remaining in the el-Fasher area, and others fleeing south to Tawila and Dar al-Salam.

The violence continued to engulf el-Fasher and its surrounding displacement camps over the following months.

With Zamzam under its control, the RSF launched an attack on el-Fasher in August 2025, and soon captured the Abu Shouk camp.

The UN Human Rights Office said at least 40 displaced people were killed inside Abu Shouk, while 19 others were injured. The International Organization for Migration reported that at least 500 residents fled the camp that day.

The RSF captured el-Fasher itself on October 26, 2025. More than 6,000 people are believed to have been killed in the attack, in el-Fasher as well as on escape routes out of the city. The UN found that RSF fighters targeted civilians, including members of non-Arab communities, and committed acts amounting to war crimes.

The RSF has previously denied targeting civilians in Zamzam and el-Fasher, while acknowledging that some fighters committed abuses.

The survivors of Zamzam, al-Shouk, and el-Fasher focus on bearing witness to the tragedy they faced.

Jumaa said the destruction of Zamzam marked not the end of the violence, but the beginning of another wave of displacement.

For him, the camp survives in the memories of those who once lived there – even as they are now displaced elsewhere.

Musa, meanwhile, said he cannot forget the first days of the siege, and the bodies he saw on the streets.

“Whoever survives must tell the story of what happened,” Musa said.

articles.title: 'Brilliant' Stoke-on-Trent theatre honoured with national award
articles.summary: Claybody Theatre is recognised during the inaugural Great British Theatres Awards.
articles.body:
The co-artistic director of a theatre based in a former potbank shed has hailed it as a "brilliant" space after it won a national award.

Claybody Theatre has been based at the Dipping House at the old Spode Works ceramics factory in Stoke-on-Trent since 2017.

It transformed the disused industrial building into a permanent 130-seat theatre after a decade of producing work in temporary spaces.

On Monday, Claybody Theatre received the honour for Great Found Space at the Great British Theatres Awards, which were held in London.

The venue was praised by the awards for having a home that strengthens the city's cultural offer and demonstrating the potential of repurposed buildings.

Co-artistic director Deb McAndrew told BBC Radio Stoke they did not expect to win because of the strong competition.

On the theatre itself, she said: "It's just a brilliant, beautiful old bit of potbank. We love it and our audiences love it."

McAndrew, who founded Claybody with fellow artistic director Conrad Nelson, described the theatre as a "very democratic" and accessible space.

"There are lots of people in a place like Stoke-on-Trent who don't feel like theatre is for them," she added. "They don't feel that theatre buildings are a threshold they can cross.

"It's a shame because there are some fantastic theatres in the area."

To try and encourage more people through the doors who otherwise would not usually go to a theatre, McAndrew said they kept prices as low as they could so "cost isn't a barrier to access".

She also said there was no "cultural barrier", adding: "Every person in north Staffordshire is one person away from Spode.

"They either knew someone who worked here or they worked here themselves or their granny worked here."

articles.title: South Carolina shrimpers weigh costs, vote in crucial US midterms
articles.summary: Shrimpers worry about fuel costs, tariffs and Trump’s proposed cuts to the agency that provides vital weather data.
articles.body:
Mount Pleasant, South Carolina – For Mark Marhefka, the weather can be the difference between a profitable fishing trip and a dangerous one.

As a shrimper and fisherman for 49 years, Marhefka relies on forecasts, weather buoys and data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to decide when it is safe to take his boats offshore. With storms and warm water temperatures disrupting this year’s fishing season, he worries that President Donald Trump’s proposed funding cuts could further reduce the services fishermen depend on.

“They’ve already started cutting back on NOAA, and they’re looking to do more in this next fiscal year,” Marhefka, who owns Abundant Seafood, told Al Jazeera. “It’s definitely something that we need to fight against.”

Since Trump returned to office in January 2025, NOAA has lost roughly 20 percent of its workforce, according to an analysis of federal employment data. The administration’s proposed 2027 budget would cut funding for ocean monitoring and terminate a programme supporting regional ocean observations.

But the weather is only one of the pressures facing South Carolina shrimpers as they head to the polls on Tuesday for the US midterm elections.

Rising fuel prices, equipment costs and competition from imported shrimp are weighing on people who make their living from the water.

Marhefka believes Democrats could address these pressures better than Republicans.

“Fuel costs have doubled since Trump has been back in office,” said Marhefka. “I voted Democrat because I really think Annie Andrews is going to help South Carolina.”

At an election-eve rally in Charleston on Monday, the state’s Democratic Senate candidate, Annie Andrews, sought to appeal to voters like Marhefka, arguing that her campaign would address the financial pressures facing coastal communities.

“I’m fighting for a South Carolina that we can afford,” Andrews said to the crowd. “I’m fighting to lower the damn diesel for our farmers and our fishermen and our shrimpers.”

Although shrimpers make up a small share of South Carolina’s electorate, their concerns raise bigger questions about the cost of doing business and retirement planning.

John Henry Middleton, an 81-year-old fisherman who has been shrimping for about 50 years, is an undecided voter. He says he is frustrated with both parties, arguing that politicians make promises but fail to work together on issues affecting common people.

“I want to see them get together and work for the good of the people,” he told Al Jazeera.

His concerns as he heads to the ballot box on Tuesday include the cost of living and whether he will have enough money to support himself in retirement. He said he has paid taxes and worked for decades, but still has to work at 81.

Kevin S, who declined to give his last name, works at Geechee Seafood on Shem Creek and said he plans to vote Republican on Tuesday. He said many people in the fishing industry lean Republican because they see government regulation as an obstacle to making a living.

“It’s a pretty regulated industry. A lot of red tape, a lot of extreme permits,” he told Al Jazeera, adding that some fishing permits can cost thousands of dollars.

Kevin added that rising fuel prices have increased the cost of running his business, but he doesn’t closely follow the factors driving those increases.

When asked whether the war in Iran was contributing to higher prices, he said he didn’t know enough about the issue to say. Instead, he pointed to Trump’s efforts to increase domestic energy production as a reason he thinks Republicans are better placed to address fuel costs.

He also believes many blue-collar workers share this view, but emphasised that industry support for Republicans does not necessarily mean enthusiasm for the party.

“I just don’t really trust Democrats as much to make the best financial decisions,” he said. “It’s not that a lot of people love the Republican Party. It’s more of a lesser of two evils.”

The pressures facing shrimpers are also evident in the dwindling number of businesses around Shem Creek, a historic fishing area near Charleston. Cindy and Taylor Tarvin, co-owners of Tarvin Seafood, estimate that only about eight shrimpers remain in the area. They say the decline reflects how difficult it has become to make a living in the industry.

“Younger captains can make a living, but not a lavish one,” Cindy Tarvin told Al Jazeera.

The Tarvins said their diesel costs rose sharply this year. They started the year paying $2.71 per gallon (3.78 litres), but by late September they were paying $5.99 per gallon. The American Automobile Association (AAA) reported that South Carolina’s average retail diesel price reached a record $6.17 that month.

Maintenance and equipment costs have also risen, adding to the financial strain on boat owners.

“There will always be a demand for watermen and what they produce. What scale they’re able to do it at is the big question,” Taylor Tarvin told Al Jazeera.

The Tarvins agree that one of the biggest challenges is the volume of imported shrimp entering the US market. Shrimp from abroad is often sold at lower prices, making it difficult for domestic fishermen to compete.

They said the influx of imports has contributed to falling prices and razor-thin profit margins, forcing some local boats out of business.

The competition extends well beyond South Carolina. According to the Southern Shrimp Alliance, the United States imported 1.59 billion pounds, or about 721,000 tonnes, of frozen warmwater shrimp in 2025, a 2 percent increase from the previous year.

In July 2026, the Trump administration imposed additional tariffs of 10 to 12.5 percent on imported shrimp from major suppliers including India, Ecuador, Indonesia, Vietnam and Thailand.

Trump’s tariffs on imported shrimp initially raised hopes among domestic shrimpers that foreign products would become more expensive and local catch more competitive. But the Tarvins said they have yet to see a meaningful benefit in the prices they receive, and are unsure whether they ever will.

There is another complication. Tariffs on imported steel, aluminium and products made from those materials have increased the cost of maintaining boats.

“So all of the pieces and parts that go into keeping a fishing boat running and keeping the equipment replaceable are affected by tariffs,” Cindy said.

For Marhefka, rising costs are part of a broader frustration with the country’s direction. He says he tries not to discuss politics often, but has heard growing frustration from those who voted for Trump and feel their circumstances have worsened.

“I just don’t think that we can go and handle another two more years of this,” he said. “We’re just getting squeezed too hard.”

articles.title: Trump’s tariff claims need evidence, not a rubber stamp
articles.summary: Congress gave the International Trade Commission the responsibility to establish the facts, not validate the president’s conclusions.
articles.body:
President Trump’s Canada tariffs are headed to court . But the judiciary isn’t the only institution that should scrutinize his claims of foreign discrimination. Congress assigned that responsibility to an independent trade commission for a reason.

The International Trade Commission must act as an independent investigator, not a source of institutional legitimacy for conclusions the administration has already reached.

The commission is seeking public comments on how it should implement Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 , the long-dormant statute Trump invoked to impose tariffs of up to 50 percent. What qualifies as discrimination? What evidence is required? Should the commission’s findings be public?

The answers to these questions will test whether the International Trade Commission’s independence means anything.

When Congress drafted Section 338’s predecessor, Section 317 of the Tariff Act of 1922 , it could have left investigations to an executive agency that the president preferred. Instead, it assigned the job to an independent Tariff Commission, today’s International Trade Commission. That was a deliberate institutional choice. The point was to separate the facts from the politics.

Start with discrimination. Trump increasingly treats any disadvantage facing American exporters as evidence of foreign discrimination. The commission should distinguish unequal commercial outcomes from discrimination in fact. Consider Canada, where European cheese exporters enjoy preferences negotiated under the Canada-European Union Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement. American exporters receive different treatment under the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement.

The administration calls that discrimination . But trade agreements result from bargaining. The EU negotiated its preferences in exchange for other concessions. The U.S. negotiated a different deal. Just because European exporters secured more favorable treatment doesn’t automatically mean American exporters are being discriminated against.

Congress anticipated this distinction. In 1922, the Senate struck a clause that would have made any failure to give American commerce equal treatment grounds for action and kept a test of discrimination instead. As Barry Appleton of New York Law School explains , Congress did not enact the broader equal treatment provision it considered.

Trade scholar Simon Lester has similarly argued that unequal effects alone should not establish discrimination under Section 338. The International Trade Commission should examine a measure’s design, structure and application to determine whether it discriminates in fact against American commerce, placing it at a demonstrable disadvantage relative to comparable foreign commerce.

Otherwise, Section 338 becomes a most-favored-nation clause that nobody signed, allowing Washington to claim concessions that others negotiated without offering anything in return. The commission should ask whether these differences satisfy the statute’s definition of discrimination, not simply whether American exporters would prefer a better deal.

The same rigor is also needed when countries retaliate against American tariffs. If a foreign government targets U.S. products in response to Trump’s tariffs, is that discrimination within the statute’s meaning? That conclusion requires an investigation, not simply a change in terminology from “retaliation” to “discrimination.”

What about evidence? The commission should require more than mere allegations of unfair treatment. It should identify the foreign measure, establish how American commerce is treated differently from that of other countries and demonstrate the resulting commercial disadvantage.

It should also consider alternative explanations. Market share can decline for reasons unrelated to discrimination. Regulations can fetter American exporters without being discriminatory per commitments rather than hostility toward American commerce.

Most importantly, the International Trade Commission should assess the magnitude of any demonstrated disadvantage. This is where Section 338’s language becomes especially important.

Congress authorized duties of up to 50 percent to “offset” the burden or disadvantage of foreign discrimination. Trump’s initial Section 338 action against Canada imposed the statutory maximum on roughly $20 billion in imports , citing alleged discrimination involving automobiles , dairy and alcohol . Yet the tariffs covered a much broader assortment of Canadian products. How does a 50 percent tariff on those goods offset the particular disadvantage allegedly suffered by American exporters? Why wouldn’t 15 or 25 percent suffice?

Those are precisely the questions an independent Commission should ask. There is a difference between compensating for lost export opportunities, protecting American industries from import competition and exerting economic pressure to secure concessions. The president may prefer the last objective. But Section 338’s requirement to offset a disadvantage cannot simply be ignored.

Finally, the International Trade Commission’s findings and recommendations should be public. The commission can use established procedures for trade investigations, including published standards, opportunities for public comment and hearings. The justification for imposing tariffs on Americans does not deserve secrecy.

The courts will have to decide whether the commission’s findings must precede presidential action. But the point is that its independent fact-finding isn’t an obstacle to effective trade enforcement. It’s what gives its findings credibility.

Congress gave the International Trade Commission the responsibility to establish the facts, not to validate the president’s conclusions. A century later, the commission should demonstrate why that distinction matters.

Marc L. Busch is the Karl F. Landegger Professor of International Business Diplomacy at the Walsh School of Foreign Service, Georgetown University.

articles.title: Specialist equipment to deal with future drone threat in Jersey
articles.summary: The equipment will help authorities detect, assess and respond to future drone reports.
articles.body:
Authorities in Jersey have got new equipment to detect, assess and respond to future drone reports.

Flights were affected on Friday and Saturday evening at the island's airport, causing major disruption. Police said an investigation was under way.

There is increasing use of the small unmanned aircraft for filming, photography and light displays, but strict rules are employed to keep airspace and maritime space safe and functional.

Minister for Justice and Home Affairs Helen Miles said: "Protecting public safety and maintaining Jersey's connectivity remain our priorities. We will continue to work with police, Ports of Jersey and partners to ensure the island is as well prepared as possible."

Drones are not allowed to be flown within two nautical miles (2.3miles/3.7km) of Jersey, Guernsey and Alderney airports unless the Office of the Director of Civil Aviation and local air traffic control have granted permission.

Jersey Police have also confirmed that an RAF plane which landed in the island on Sunday evening was due to the threat of drones affecting the airport.

Police said they were still trying to find out who was responsible and asked anyone with any information about any incidents, no matter how significant, to get in contact.

Islanders, airlines and travellers have been reassured that Jersey is alert, its response has been strengthened, and agencies were prepared to respond to any further reports, emergency sevices said.

articles.title: 'One of the worst': Over 30 killed, 45 missing after Russian strikes on Ukraine aid distribution site
articles.summary: At least 31 people were killed after Russian strikes hit a site distributing humanitarian aid in southern Ukraine, with more than 45 residents still
articles.body: At least 31 people were killed after Russian strikes hit a site distributing humanitarian aid in southern Ukraine, with more than 45 residents still missing as rescue teams searched through the rubble, officials said on Tuesday.The attacks took place on Monday in Komyshuvakha village in the Zaporizhzhia region, targeting a former school being used to distribute humanitarian assistance and a nearby shelter. People had gathered in a queue to collect aid when the strikes hit. AP reported.Emergency workers and volunteers continued searching the heavily damaged sites, where explosions had left craters. Rescuers recovered bodies from the debris, while at least five people were injured.“The scale of the tragedy is terrifying,” Mykhailo Semikin, acting head of the region’s military administration, said in an online post. “This is one of the worst tragedies in terms of the number of civilian victims in our region since the start of the full-scale war.”Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the former school, where humanitarian aid was regularly distributed, was struck first, followed by an attack on the shelter nearby.Russian attacks hit hospitals and energy infrastructureThe strikes in Zaporizhzhia came amid a wider wave of Russian attacks across Ukraine overnight into Tuesday, targeting power plants, damaging medical facilities and injuring scores of people. AP reported.Russia launched 289 attack drones, 17 ballistic missiles and 59 cruise missiles across nine regions, Zelenskyy said in an online post. The barrage triggered emergency power cuts and coincided with the US midterm elections, he added.“The Russians think America won’t notice this signal of theirs,” Zelenskyy said. “But we need to notice and stop such terror. We need to help Ukraine defend its skies; otherwise, Russia will never stop its missile strikes.”In the northeastern Kharkiv region, at least 62 people were injured in a Russian missile and drone attack, local authorities said. A medical facility in the Nemyshlianskyi district was damaged, while windows were shattered in four apartment buildings and several cars were damaged.More than 200 patients had to be moved to other medical facilities, Oleh Syniehubov, head of the regional military administration, said.In the Dnipro area, a Russian attack killed one person and injured 17, local authorities said. Rescuers pulled a woman alive from the rubble on Tuesday morning.The attack damaged an outpatient clinic and a hospital, forcing patients to be transferred to other hospitals, Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the regional military administration, said.Attacks follow end of Oleshky ceasefireThe latest attacks came after the expiry of a six-day ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which had allowed residents trapped there to evacuate. The truce was the most significant between Kyiv and Moscow since 2022.Zelenskyy said Ukraine had proposed extending the ceasefire, but Russia responded with further attacks.“We offered to Russia to extend the cease-fire in Oleshky, but this was the answer: new attacks, new strikes, new killings of our people,” he said in Berlin, where he was meeting German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.The attacks also came as Ukraine prepared for another round of US-brokered peace negotiations next week, more than four and a half years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion.You use AI every day. articles.title: Escaped Tennessee inmate captured, authorities say
articles.summary: Jacob Allen Morley, the convicted murderer who escaped from a Tennessee prison, is in custody, the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation said Tuesday.
articles.body: Jacob Allen Morley, the convicted murderer who escaped from a Tennessee prison, is in custody, the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation said Tuesday. The capture came more than a week after he escaped on Oct. 25 from the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville — a town of about 3,500, roughly 100 miles north of Memphis — and allegedly stole a truck that was later found abandoned in Illinois. The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation announced that Morley was captured near Kansas City, Missouri, and was in custody on Tuesday. The Missouri State Highway Patrol said it received information from the TBI at around 9:30 a.m. Tuesday that Morley may have been traveling west on Interstate 70 near Independence, according to a statement. Morley’s vehicle was located by Flock Safety cameras, the statement said. Officers from multiple agencies moved into the area as it “was believed the suspect was armed with multiple weapons,” the statement said. A police helicopter then spotted Morley’s car and followed it. Morley’s car “attempted to travel off the roadway and became stuck, at which time a trooper with the Patrol confronted Morley and took him into custody without incident,” the statement said. He was taken into custody on Tuesday around 11:34 a.m., police said. Prison officials discovered Morley, 28, was missing around 11:30 p.m. on Oct. 25. Security video showed he had breached a perimeter fence, the Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement. “He has been added to the Tennessee Most Wanted list and should be considered dangerous,” it said. Morley was convicted in 2025 of murder, abuse of a corpse, tampering with evidence and aggravated burglary in the killing of co-worker Cody Birchfield, 34, in 2022, according to court documents shared by the Carter County Clerk’s Office in Tennessee. In an interview with NBC News, Birchfield’s sister, Carrie Norman, called her brother’s killer “a very dangerous man.” “And if he gets ahold of any kind of weapon, he will kill somebody,” she said. In a statement Tuesday afternoon after Morley was taken into custody, Norman thanked the authorities and everyone who followed the case. The white Ford F-350 truck that Morley allegedly stole had passed the Hornbeak Fire Department in the town of Hornbeak, Tennessee, shortly after the theft early Monday. Hornbreak is 12 miles east of Tiptonville. The fire department on its Facebook page posted timestamped still images from security video showing the truck driving by. The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation said Tuesday that the truck was found abandoned in Marion, Illinois, about 123 miles north of Hornbeak. It was left behind a business, police there and in Tennessee said. Morley was accused of shooting Birchfield in the back of the head. Birchfield’s body was found in a large metal box under Morley’s residence in northeast Tennessee, court documents state. A motive was unclear, and Morley claimed self-defense during trial. He reported that had been hospitalized multiple times for mental health issues, including bipolar disorder, and had no prior felony offenses, according to the records. Morley was sentenced to life in prison following his conviction.

articles.title: Greenland parliament approves security deal with US, Denmark
articles.summary: Lawmakers vote 16-0 for trilateral agreement signed in September, while seven abstained.
articles.body:
Lawmakers in the semi-autonomous Danish territory of Greenland have approved an agreement with Denmark and the United States aimed at bolstering security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.

The deal was passed 16-0 on Tuesday, with seven lawmakers abstaining.

The agreement was signed in September by US President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

It followed months of negotiations behind the scenes amid growing tensions over Trump’s repeated threats to seize the vast, resource-rich Arctic island.

Greenlandic Foreign Minister Mute Egede said the ratification was another important step for the self-governing island.

“The road to this point has been ⁠a difficult one for us as ⁠a people. But we have stood firm on our fundamental principles, chosen dialogue and taken responsibility for our country’s interests,” he wrote in a ⁠post on Facebook.

“This is about all of us. The Greenland we love. ⁠About our security. And about our ⁠right to shape our own future,” he said.

Located between Europe and North America, Greenland is the world’s largest island, with a population of 57,000 people.

Trump’s refusal last year to rule out a military invasion had caused fear among Greenlanders, the majority of whom rejected US control, according to opinion polls.

The trilateral deal paves the way for more US bases on Greenland. It also allows the US to “modernise and expand” its activities at the Pituffik Space Base, a remote US military installation in northwest Greenland.

Under its terms, Greenland will remain under Danish control – but the agreement would still apply if the island eventually chooses independence.

The deal stipulates it will only “enter into force” once the “necessary parliamentary processes of the Kingdom of Denmark, in conjunction with Greenland, have been completed”.

Danish lawmakers are set to debate it later this month, while no approval is required from the US Senate.
