articles.title: Google to shut off search for schools that opt out of AI
articles.summary: The company said AI-enabled products would be shut off by default for schools, which would also cut off their access to Google Search.
articles.body: Google announced Tuesday morning that it would switch off AI products by default for students in schools that use the technology giant’s education software. But those schools that forgo its AI services would also be cut off from Google Search. The move comes after mounting criticism from advocacy groups and senators about the spread of Google’s AI services available in classrooms. Until Tuesday, its AI products — branded under the Gemini moniker — were automatically activated for schools using Google Classroom. Google said Tuesday’s move would also cut off students’ access to Google Search if schools do not enable Gemini, given AI’s growing integration into the company’s search products. Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president and general manager of education, said in a blog post announcing the change that access to Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search “will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn them on.” “We believe schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach,” Phillips wrote. Some education and technology advocates immediately slammed the decision, painting the move as a punishment for schools that don’t use Google’s AI. “It is unfortunate that Google has prioritized its business interests over the education of our children,” said Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers, a national educators union. “Instead of working with teachers and parents to uphold privacy and ensure their tools are safe and useful, it throws the baby out with the bathwater and bans access to the tools altogether,” she told NBC News in written comments. Josh Golin, executive director of advocacy group Fairplay, said in a statement that Google is attempting “to strong-arm schools into using its AI products.” “Schools should use this opportunity to help students find more privacy-protective alternatives for search, as well as ways to do more substantive research beyond search and click,” Golin said. In a statement posted to social media after this article was published, Google said the announcements “give schools more choice, not less,” and that schools can turn on Google Search individually without enabling Gemini products. But Search will still have AI features built into it, which the company said have been updated “to make it better for learning. Specifically, AI Mode and AI Overviews will offer step-by-step guided learning through problems, so that students don’t get quick answers to schoolwork.” Earlier this year, Google turned on Gemini in its Classroom app, allowing children — regardless of age — to access AI products unless districts disabled it. Parent advocacy groups and experts on the use of technology in schools denounced Google for providing AI products to children — raising concern that students would outsource their work to AI systems on school devices — and lobbied school districts to disable Gemini products. In an open letter in early October, 13 leading parent advocacy organizations — including the Digital Childhood Institute and Schools Beyond Screens — called on school districts to turn off access to Gemini and YouTube, which is also owned by Google. Google has established a dominant role in education technology over the past 15 years. The vast majority of Chromebook laptops are purchased by school districts to provide to students. Nearly two-thirds of assignments use a Google product, according to a 2023 report by the firm Schoolytics. This year, the company began offering multiday AI training sessions for educators, featuring sessions that focused on how they could mitigate pushback by teachers who don’t want to use AI. Research on AI in educational settings has not established a long-term benefit for students. There are no high-quality causal studies into student use of AI, according to the SCALE Initiative at the Stanford Graduate School of Education. Researchers have also warned that many of the studies conducted so far on AI in education didn’t measure whether it boosted learning and often did not test whether AI-assisted learning was superior to other teaching methods. In Tuesday’s blog post, Google said that for schools that enable its AI products, it will now detect when a student is trying to use them just to get an answer on an assignment. A redesigned version of Google Search will instead walk students through the topic or problem and work through the concepts, without going directly to the answer, the company said.

articles.title: UK’s King Charles expresses ‘sorrow’ in Antigua over slave trade
articles.summary: Caribbean nations call for reparations as King Charles stops short of issuing an apology for colonial-era slavery.
articles.body:
King Charles III has said at the official opening of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda that the transatlantic slave trade fills him with “horror” and “the most profound personal sorrow”.

The British monarch said on Tuesday that the slave trade “still casts a shadow over these [Caribbean] islands and other members of our Commonwealth”, and that the Royal Navy had played “a leading role” in ending it.

“We cannot change the actions of those who came before us,” Charles said. “We can, however, learn from the past.”

The king said he was seeking ways to address the wrongs by improving access to education, investing in jobs, encouraging trade among Commonwealth countries and pushing for climate resilience.

He ended the speech short of the apology that many Caribbean and African countries had hoped for. He offered no measures to address the economic and social damage of slavery.

Buckingham Palace had said the king would not issue a formal apology for slavery during his Caribbean tour, which also took him to the Bahamas and Guyana.

Guyanese President Mohamed Irfaan Ali said in an interview that an apology should be the king’s next step.

The dispute surfaced at the last Commonwealth summit in Samoa in 2024, when leaders called for discussions about reparations despite opposition from then-British Prime Minister Keir Starmer.

Last week, current British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK was open to a formal apology , while ruling out financial reparations.

Burnham, writing in The Guardian, said he wanted “to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people”.

He also proposed leading a programme of debt restructuring to help the Commonwealth’s poorest countries.

Ahead of Charles’s speech on Tuesday, a small group of protesters outside the venue held signs reading “Acknowledge the wrong. Commit to repair.”

“Technically, we’re free, but mentally a lot of us aren’t,” said Shana Michelle, from Antigua. “You have to apologise, yes. That is where we start with the repair.”

Leaders, including Burnham, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, were among those in attendance on Tuesday.

The Commonwealth has 56 member nations. Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne said, “No nation should be forced to mortgage its future simply to survive its present.”

articles.title: Ryanair passenger describes 'traumatic' Murcia flight bomb threat
articles.summary: Sarah Jones says passengers had to wait in a hangar for three hours after landing at Murcia in Spain.
articles.body:
The evacuation of a Ryanair aircraft after a suspected bomb threat has been described as "quite traumatic" by a passenger who was on board the flight.

Sarah Jones said police, fire crews and bomb disposal officers surrounded the plane after it landed at Murcia airport from Manchester.

The medic from Manchester said she and her fellow passengers were told to leave their belongings on board and then spent about three hours in an airport hangar while the plane was searched.

Spanish officials said no explosives were found. The aircraft was one of seven searched at airports across Europe following a series of suspected bomb threats.

Jones was travelling with colleagues Charlotte and Kelly to work as medics at a golf tournament in La Manga in south-eastern Spain.

She said the flight was uneventful until the aircraft landed at about 10:30 local time (09:30 GMT).

"When we landed, the plane just sort of stopped really quickly and we were held there for a while," she told the BBC.

Passengers initially thought they were waiting for permission to taxi to the terminal.

"Then we were just surrounded by police, the bomb squad, ambulances were there, fire engines," she said.

"Then we were told that we needed to evacuate the plane, but we weren't allowed to bring anything off.

"We had to leave the luggage in the overhead lockers."

Jones said passengers walked towards the airport and were initially given little information about what had happened.

She said a police officer told her there had been a security threat, but would not confirm whether it involved the airport or the plane.

They were later told there had been a bomb threat made against their aircraft, Jones said.

She said sniffer dogs searched the plane and passengers' luggage was checked.

"I think we were more frustrated that we didn't know what was going on," she said.

Jones said passengers remained calm but spent time outside in hot weather before being offered water.

They were eventually allowed to return to the plane through its rear door to collect their luggage, before leaving through the front door and going through the airport.

Jones said they did not leave the airport until after 14:00 local time.

Spanish officials said 121 people, including crew, had been on board the flight.

Other aircraft were inspected in Poland, Italy and Bulgaria.

It is not known whether the threats were connected.

The UK government described the incidents as "malicious hoax threats" and said it had well-tested procedures for handling potential aviation threats.

articles.title: In 1940, fire destroyed the dome and grand rooms of England’s Castle Howard; the family restored fire-damaged interiors, reopening selected rooms in 2025
articles.summary: Discover the remarkable restoration journey of Castle Howard, which survived a devastating fire in 1940 and underwent continuous renovation to unveil its stunning interiors in 2025. Explore its rich history and architectural significance.
articles.body: The dome of Castle Howard collapsed into the Great Hall after a fire broke out on 9 November 1940. Flames spread from a chimney and, by extension, destroyed more than 20 rooms in the North Yorkshire House. The structure became a testimony to how a house can survive a fire and still carry its consequences for generations. The damage left a substantial part of the building in need of restoration. The latest phase, unveiled in 2025, retrieved long-lost decorative features to view and brought rooms affected by the fire back into the visitor experience.A fire that altered the house Well before the smoke cleared from the 1940 flames, the Howards of Castle Howard had already lived a lifetime. The fire was just a bookmark in the chapters of Castle Howard’s history; its story started when the 3rd Earl of Carlisle commissioned John Vanbrugh in 1699, along with architect Nicholas Hawksmoor. But Vanbrugh’s untimely death in 1726, before the house was complete, coupled with the 3rd Earl’s death in 1738, dampened its future. The house turned a new leaf when it passed into the next phase of development under the stewardship of the 4th Earl of Carlisle.The west wing was designed in a Palladian style by Sir Thomas Robinson, according to the estate’s official history. The Long Gallery was completed between 1801 and 1811, and further tuning up ensued between 1870 and 1875. These stages took place like instalments and rendered Castle Howard with architectural work that endured for more than a century, rather than a single, uninterrupted building campaign. The estate’s official history, the building of Castle Howard, records these changes and the later conservation which followed.The fire also took much of the house’s historical contents with it, and rooms that had formed part of the house for generations were lost. Girls evacuated from Queen Margaret’s School helped salvage possessions from the burning building.Restoration did not end with the immediate aftermath. The ancestral home finally opened up to the public in 1952. Work on the dome took place between 1960 and 1962. The Garden Hall was completed in 1981, and the central block was re-roofed in 1994-95. Its later debut and appearance on the screen brought a revitalisation to its rooms and architecture. Castle Howard became associated with the television adaptation of Brideshead Revisited and more recently, with Bridgerton.The rooms restored in 2025 Castle Howard opened a newly restored group of interiors to visitors on 25 April 2025. The work included the Tapestry Drawing Room, the Grand Staircase and the Long Gallery. Smithsonian Magazine’s article from the same date and year described the reopening and the family’s continuing effort to repair the house.The Tapestry Drawing Room had been gutted in the fire, and reconstruction had not taken place afterwards. After the restoration, it returned to its original 18th-century look with four tapestries woven by John Vanderbank in 1706, according to Castle Howard’s announcement. The scene embodies the four seasons and derives from works by David Teniers.The Grand staircase, dating from the 1870s, was also rearranged. It now displays objects associated with the Grand Tour, alongside new plaster casts and busts. The Long Gallery was rehung with Italian Paintings of Rome by Giovanni Paolo Pannini, commissioned by the 4th Earl of Carlisle, as well as portraits of the family.Castle Howard’s official announcement credits architect Francis Terry as the project lead, with designers Remy Renzullo and Alec Cobbe, who dressed the interiors, alongside specialist craftspeople. articles.title: A Norfolk farmer’s doorstop was a 68 cm Bronze Age dagger, bent for ritual burial; one of just six known in Europe, it sold to a museum for £40,970
articles.summary: A farmer in Norfolk unknowingly used a rare Bronze Age ceremonial dagger as a doorstop for nearly a decade. Now identified as one of only six in Europe, the Rudham Dirk was sold to Norwich Castle Museum for £40,970, with help from a significant grant.
articles.body: If farmers work the land long enough, they become used to the plough throwing up strange metal objects. It hardly merits a second glance and is mostly made up of rusting machinery or the parts of a long-forgotten gate. But now and then, something far stranger and older emerges, and whether or not anyone notices depends solely on who happens to be standing close by. Before anyone realised what it was, a bent green piece of metal that appeared in a field in North Norfolk held a door open for around ten years. The fact that it was eventually acknowledged and placed in a museum serves as a helpful reminder of how much history can be found in plain sight.The object is a ceremonial dagger known as the Rudham Dirk, and it is one of only six of its kind known in Europe. Norwich Castle Museum bought it from the landowner for £40,970, helped by a grant of almost £39,000 from the National Heritage Memorial Fund, which stepped in so the weapon could go on public display in Norfolk.A find nobody recognisedThe dagger was found during ploughing at East Rudham in 2002 or 2003. The farmer who discovered it did not recognise its archaeological importance and took it to his farm office, where he used it as a doorstop. It remained there until 2013, when he finally showed it to specialists from Norfolk's Identification and Recording Service. They recognised it as an exceptionally rare Middle Bronze Age ceremonial object.That changed in 2013 when it was shown to the Identification and Recording Service in Norfolk, which administers the county's branch of the Portable Antiquities Scheme. The initiative is in place to record archaeological finds made by members of the public and its staff dated the dagger and classified it as a significant artefact. At the time, reports said the owner had considered throwing it out, but a friend advised an expert should take a look at it first.Why it was so unusualWhen straightened out, the Rudham Dirk would have been about 68 cm long: roughly three times the size of a standard Bronze Age dirk. It dates back to the Middle Bronze Age, about 1500 BC. It was so big and hefty that it would have been useless in a fight. The blade was never sharpened, and there are no rivet holes to attach a handle; thus, it was clearly made as a ceremonial piece and not as a practical weapon. Curators are almost positive that is why it was found folded in half. It was deliberately bent, part of the ritual destruction of metalwork before burial, a process well known from the Bronze Age.There are only six dirks of this type known in Europe, two from France, two from the Netherlands and two from Britain. The other British case was likewise in Norfolk. The British Museum believes that it had been placed vertically into soft peaty earth approximately 3,500 years earlier and that a man wandering in woodlands near Oxborough tripped over it in 1988. Such a dirk would have weighed 2.37 kilogrammes (5.2 pounds) and measured 70.9 centimetres (27.9 inches) long, too unwieldy to be of practical use. Museum curators suggest that it may have been manufactured for ceremonial purposes or as a store of riches. Its catalogue article adds that the Oxborough dirk and its four continental parallels are so similar that they may all have been made in a single workshop, though nobody can say whether that workshop stood in Britain or across the water.Keeping it in NorfolkA lone bronze dirk did not fall under England's Treasure Act, which requires finds to have two or more bronze pieces or at least one thing composed of precious metal, according to a research chapter released by Sidestone. The owner has no legal duty to pass it over and any acquisition would be a matter of negotiation.Norwich Castle Museum and Art Gallery negotiated with the landowner and agreed to purchase the dirk for £40,970. The National Heritage Memorial Fund contributed a grant of £38,970, while the Norfolk and Norwich Archaeological Society provided an additional £2,000. Together, these contributions covered the full purchase price. The National Heritage Memorial Fund said its trustees wanted to secure the object for public display and ensure it remained in Norfolk. Unlike the earlier Oxborough dirk, which is held by the British Museum in London, the Rudham Dirk would stay in the county where it was discovered. Norwich Castle Museum planned to display it permanently in its archaeology galleries.Dr Tim Pestell, the museum's senior curator of archaeology, said the discovery offered insight into the beliefs and contacts of people during the Middle Bronze Age. He also hoped that displaying the object would help residents and visitors understand the region's ancient history. The Rudham Dirk is significant not only because of its unusual size but also because of what its deliberate bending reveals about Bronze Age ritual practices. Its blunt blade and lack of handle fittings suggest it was never intended for ordinary combat. Its acquisition by Norwich Castle Museum also ensured that an exceptionally rare archaeological find remained in the region where it was discovered.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Spanish transport minister resigns days after deadly train crash
articles.summary: At least 69 people were killed and dozens injured in the collision south of the capital, Madrid.
articles.body:
Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente has resigned - six days after the high-speed train collision in which at least 69 people were killed and dozens injured.

He announced his decision in Congress, after giving evidence on last Wednesday's disaster near the town of Urda, south of the capital Madrid, in which a train smashed into the back of a stationary train.

"A transport minister in a country like Spain cannot remain in office after two accidents of this seriousness in less than a year," he said - a reference to January's crash on the same line which left 46 people dead.

Last week's crash was one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013.

Puente announced his decision at the end of a lengthy congressional session on Tuesday evening in which he had outlined new rail safety measures and had been grilled by the opposition.

He also said: "I am not only stepping down from my position as minister of transport, but... I am also withdrawing my name from the lists for the early legislative elections."

Puente's position immediately came under scrutiny after the 28 October crash.

The main opposition, the conservative People's Party (PP) and the far-right Vox, were both calling for his resignation - as were some of the government's allies.

They argued that the minister should take responsibility for a high-speed rail system that many Spaniards now regard as unsafe and whose credibility even Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez admitted was "broken".

The opposition also criticised Puente for appearing to blame human error for the crash, claiming the minister was trying to deflect the blame from his own failings.

But, having said he was going to remain in his post just a few days ago, his resignation appears to have taken many by surprise.

The rail accident and Puente's decision have come at a crucial moment in the Spanish political calendar, with early general elections on 29 November.

Many observers see the accident as a massive electoral setback to the Socialist-led government that will make it impossible for Sánchez to defy the polls and win the election.

Puente's predicament presented him and the prime minister with a dilemma - refusing to resign might look insensitive in the wake of the accident and stepping down could look like acknowledging he and the government were at fault.

In the end, Puente opted for the second option, insisting his decision had been driven by "political dignity".

The prime minister praised his colleague who had "faced up to the situation, provided answers and solutions, and then stepped aside".

"Out of dignity. Of his own accord. Out of respect for the victims," Sánchez added.

Many Spaniards will now ask whether Puente's successors will manage to restore faith in the country's railway system.

Last Wednesday's accident involved a train run by state-owned operator Renfe with 397 passengers on board and a stationary train run by private operator Iryo, which was carrying 147 passengers.

A reported issue with the automatic signalling system - a computer failure - had forced all trains to halt on the affected stretch.

Leaked audio recordings published in Spanish media soon after the crash revealed conversations between train drivers and a control centre just minutes before the disaster.

The three recordings of conversations between Madrid's control centre and two train drivers appear to show that the Renfe train was given clearance to move even though the other train had stopped on the track, about 25km (15 miles) ahead.

In one, a control centre operator is speaking to the driver of the Renfe train, which was having some technical difficulties.

After some exchanges, the control operator tells the driver: "Continue your journey and then proceed under [Lateral Signalling Block], at normal speed with normal operation."

The driver replies: "At normal speed?" To which the controller answers: "Yes."

The Lateral Signalling Block is a back-up system used when the automatic signalling or data transmission system fails.

The driver of the stationary Iryo train says in another audio recording that communication with the train-control system has been lost, and it is not moving.

The train "is stationary in front of the entry signal at Urda", the driver tells the control centre operator. After a series of exchanges, the driver is then told to "resume the journey" normally.

The Iryo driver then contacts the control centre again, according to a later recording, saying they cannot start the train. "The train won't allow me to control the [security] system. That's why I am still stopped in front of the entry signal," they say.

The latter recording suggests that the controller had been notified that the Iryo train remained stationary as the Renfe train approached.

Iryo said its carriages were "struck from behind" by the other train.

articles.title: Retired NYPD officer arrested after 'off with his head' post over Florida mosque expansion
articles.summary: Retired NYPD officer Rodolfo Mienert allegedly posted "off with his head!" on Facebook targeting a Pinellas County commissioner over a mosque vote.
articles.body: A retired NYPD officer living in Florida was arrested Monday after authorities say he made a social media post calling for the beheading of a Pinellas County commissioner who recently voted to approve the expansion of a local mosque. Rodolfo Mienert, who now lives in St. Petersburg, allegedly commented on a Facebook post criticizing Pinellas County Commissioner Brian Scott for supporting a land-use change that would allow the North Pinellas mosque to expand. According to the Pinellas County Sheriff's Office, the 68-year-old ex-officer called Scott a "Republican turncoat" before writing, "off with his head!" Mienert posted this Facebook comment under the username "Rudy MineAllmine," according to an affidavit obtained by Fox News Digital. OHIO MAN CHARGED OVER GRAPHIC THREATS TO KILL TRUMP, BEHEAD GOP LAWMAKER The account's profile picture shows Bugs Bunny holding a revolver, while its bio reads, "...if I pissed off a libtard today, I'm happy!! no further reply!!" The last post made by this account reposted a campaign video from Scott, accompanied with the message: "DO NOT vote for this person, he voted FOR a mosque." Detectives traced the IP address of the account that made the post to Mienert, who later confirmed the account was his. MAN INDICTED FOR ALLEGEDLY POSTING GRUESOME DEATH THREATS AGAINST KRISTI NOEM, PAM BONDI ON SOCIAL MEDIA Mienert told detectives he is "very vocal and not afraid to share his opinion" on political issues and said he called Scott a "turncoat" because of his vote to approve the mosque expansion. Mienert also told detectives he had attended an Oct. 27 County Commission meeting where residents discussed the mosque issue at length. During that meeting, he said he escaped New York to "beautiful Florida" and claimed the growing footprint of the mosque would damage the environment and make traffic worse. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Mienert was arrested and charged with one felony count of a written or electronic threat to kill, an offense that carries a maximum of 15 years in prison in Florida. In a statement, Pinellas County Sheriff Bob Gualtieri said that "threatening to cut off the head of a county commissioner because of his vote on a land issue is intolerable and we will strictly enforce the law against anyone who makes threats of this nature." Mienert, who retired as a sergeant after 22 years with the New York Police Department, remains in the Pinellas County Jail, according to records reviewed by Fox News Digital. He is set to appear in court Tuesday afternoon.

articles.title: Routine voting issues fuel conspiracy theories and confusion
articles.summary: Westchester County ballot tabulators malfunctioned across the county Tuesday, alarming voters and fueling a flurry of conspiracy theories online.
articles.body: SLEEPY HOLLOW, N.Y. — Westchester County ballot tabulators malfunctioned across the county Tuesday, alarming voters and fueling a flurry of conspiracy theories online. The issue was discovered early in the morning, after ballot tabulators failed to scan voters’ hand-marked paper ballots in 44 out of 45 of the county’s municipalities. State election officials said in a post on X that the issue was due to a programming error. Election officials directed voters to put their ballots in secure orange ballot bags, following standard contingency plans. Follow live updates on the midterm elections The news has raised alarm among voters and onlookers. In text chains and Facebook posts viewed by NBC News, Westchester voters discussed the issue, with some expressing concern over whether their votes would be counted. Tensions are high in part because Westchester is home to a key House race in the battle for control of Congress: In the 17th Congressional District, Republican Rep. Mike Lawler faces Democrat Cait Conley in a close race. The district narrowly leans blue, but Lawler has held it for four years by maintaining high popularity and campaigning aggressively on crime and affordability issues. Conley, a veteran and former Biden cybersecurity official, hopes to capitalize on President Donald Trump’s sagging approval ratings in her challenge. In social media posts, both candidates urged voters not to be dissuaded by the tabulator issues. Ken Jenkins, the Westchester County executive, said Tuesday afternoon that alternate tabulators are being rolled out, and that the ballots stored in secure bags will be counted after polls close at 9 p.m. “Long-established emergency ballot procedures have been implemented, where completed ballots are secured, under bipartisan control, and will be counted,” the New York State Board of Elections said in a Tuesday statement posted on X. “While technical issues can be frustrating, contingency procedures exist for precisely these circumstances.” New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, told reporters that the ballots would be counted. “Every vote will be counted; I think I need to say that three times. Every vote will be counted, every vote will be counted,” she said in Queens on Tuesday morning. “It’s being resolved in a bipartisan way that it’s supposed to. The backup plan is in place, so voters in Westchester should feel very confident.” Isolated ballot scanner issues are routine, though the problems have been been particularly common in New York state. In 2018, scanners jammed across New York City, while Queens reported tabulator issues in 2024. This year, ballot tabulator issues also occurred in other states including Florida and Oklahoma, while other issues like power outages and flooding shuttered some polling sites, including some in Maricopa County. Online influencers supportive of the Republican Party and some officials saw an opportunity in the malfunctioning machines and polling location closures, framing them as a conspiracy against party candidates. “The Democrats are already cheating,” posted Loomer Unleashed, a podcast associated with close Trump ally Laura Loomer, about power outages in Maricopa County. In reality, heavy rain and flooding have caused polling location issues across the county. The ballot counting issues in New York have sparked similar accusations, including from an elected official. “The Democrats in NY will do anything and everything to cheat,” posted Rep. Claudia Tenner, R-N.Y., the chair of the House Election Integrity Caucus. “Democrats are already trying to steal the election in New York today,” Loomer wrote on social media, her post garnering over 100,000 views. “This is how the Left steals elections,” wrote Katie Miller, conservative podcast host and wife of White House adviser Steven Miller. The nascent accusations echo similar narratives Trump and his supporters raised in past elections. The most famous of these false narratives claimed machines stole votes away from Republicans, costing them the 2020 presidential election. Yet technical failures are common, officials have warned, as are conspiracies about those malfunctions. Researchers studying false online information have been worried about the potential for such accusations to recirculate as normal glitches get misrepresented. Such narratives could pave the way toward challenging the results of the election, several researchers told NBC News ahead of the midterms. In Oklahoma City, the county’s top election official said normal issues were getting far more attention than usual. “It’s not uncommon to have some voting machines cause us a few problems early in the day. It’s a common occurrence,” said Doug Sanderson, the county’s election board secretary. “Many times we wouldn’t hear about it other than from our precinct officials. I just think perhaps the climate and the sensitivity everyone has around this election causes people to be a little bit more on edge than they normally would be.” Offline in Westchester County, voting at a Sleepy Hollow polling site at a social club called the Fraternal Order of Eagles appeared to be proceeding smoothly. A regular flow of voters trickled in and out through the lunch hour in the Hudson River Valley town, most having already heard via text message or from friends and neighbors that the scanners were not functioning. As of 12:30 p.m. ET, of the 225 people who had voted at that location, only two walked away on account of the tabulators being down. “One was pretty disrespectful,” a poll worker named Dennis told NBC News, declining to share his last name. “The other said maybe they’d come back later.”

articles.title: Spanish transport minister resigns after two deadly train crashes in one year
articles.summary: Spain’s Minister of Transport Óscar Puente announced his resignation after two deadly train crashes occurred in a single year, including one last week that killed 69 people and injured more than 200.
articles.body: Spain’s Minister of Transport Óscar Puente announced his resignation after two deadly train crashes occurred in a single year, including one last week that killed 69 people and injured more than 200. “I made the decision about my future in the first few minutes after the tragedy,” Puente told lawmakers in Madrid. “A transport minister in a country like Spain cannot remain in office after two accidents of this severity in less than a year, however different they may be and regardless of whether or not they bear direct responsibility for them.” Puente resigned six days after one train plowed into another after what authorities say was a combination of human and computer errors along a high speed railway line connecting Madrid and Andalusia. One train, operated by Spain’s national rail service, crashed into a stationary train at high speed during a safety system failure that had halted all rail traffic along the line. “There was a red signal prohibiting movement, yet the train was authorized to proceed,” Puente said last week. “It is a decision made under inexplicable circumstances.” Last week’s crash was preceded by another serious rail accident in January, where two high-speed trains collided head-on in the town of Adamuz, killing at least 41 people. At the time, it was the deadliest crash Spain had seen in more than a decade. Numerous politicians and Spain’s transport workers’ union had called on Puente to resign in the aftermath of last week’s collision. The night of the crash, police scuffled with a hundreds of protesters outside the transport ministry headquarters, some of whom carried placards demanding that Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez resign. Puente’s announcement arrives just three weeks before the country’s general elections, in which the minister said he would not be standing as a candidate. Sánchez called those elections early in the wake of several corruption scandals, a controversy over housing affordability and numerous setbacks for his socialist PSOE party in municipal elections. Sánchez praised Puente in a statement on social media, saying that the former transport minister stepped aside “out of respect for the victims and the progressive project.” “Politicians like him dignify our country and show us that not all of us are the same,” Sánchez wrote. “While some only give lessons, others give everything.” This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title: $20,000 reward offered for location of missing Missouri woman Lindsey Watts, who vanished in May 2026
articles.summary: Lindsey Watts vanished from Edina, Missouri, in May 2026. Her belongings were left behind, and her phone was located in a ditch near her home. The Knox County Sheriff’s Office is investigating her disappearance.
articles.body: Tuesday, May 19, 2026, was a rainy day in Edina, Missouri. John Watts, who owns a mowing company, says the rain disrupted his work plans that day. His daughter Lindsey worked as a dietary manager at the Blessing Center in Edina but also helped her dad with his mowing business when she wasn’t working. But because of the weather, Lindsey told him she wouldn’t be able to help that day. “And I said, ‘That’s fine. We’ll go mow tomorrow,’” John told Dateline. So 34-year-old Lindsey Watts spent May 19 working a long shift at the Blessing Center. The next morning, May 20, John texted his daughter to ask when she would be available to help with the mowing. “Asked her what time she was gonna be off ‘cause we needed to go mow that day,” he said. “And she never did text me back, which was not unusual. I thought, ‘Well, she’s probably busy or something.’” Later that day, Lindsey’s teenage daughter called John, asking if he had seen her mom. He hadn’t. So Lindsey’s parents went looking for her. When they checked the family’s Life360 app, it showed Lindsey’s location at her home. But Lindsey wasn’t there. “We searched the house and the basement and the crawl space and a couple of neighbors’ houses there, and, uh, she was nowhere to be found,” John said. Lindsey’s daughter told her grandparents that she last saw her mom between 11 and 11:30 p.m. on the night of May 19. “Her daughter said she was really tired, and [Lindsey] was actually in bed when she went in and told her that she loved her and good night,” John said. “And as far as she knows, she was gonna be sleeping.” The family also learned Lindsey hadn’t shown up for work at the Blessing Center on the 20th. As they tried to figure out where Lindsey could be, her parents began calling their other children, including Lindsey’s younger sister, Lacey Watts. “My mom got ahold of me and was like, ‘Hey, have you talked to your sister today?’” Lacey recalled. “I was like, ‘No,’ but that’s not unusual. Like, we don’t talk every single day. So I didn’t think anything of it until they were like, ‘She’s gone,’ like, ‘She’s missing.’” Lindsey’s absence was very out of character. “She’s one of the sweetest people I’ve ever met,” Lacey said. “I mean, she’d do anything for anybody. Very reliable. Whenever you needed her there, she was there.” John and his wife reported Lindsey missing to the Knox County Sheriff’s Office. According to John, authorities found Lindsey’s phone in a ditch south of her house. The phone was still working, and investigators took it to examine. Lindsey’s other belongings, including her wallet, money, car, and car keys, were all found at the home. John says it did not look like there was any sort of struggle inside the house. The Knox County Sheriff’s Office led the investigation, working with the Missouri Highway Patrol and other nearby agencies, including the Kirksville Police Department and the Lewis County Sheriff’s Department, to search for Lindsey, according to John. “They’ve pretty much done all the footwork,” he said. “They have not found anything yet.” Dateline called Sheriff Carl Knoche at the Knox County Sheriff’s Office for an update on the investigation into Lindsey’s disappearance and has not yet heard back. John told Dateline there’s been no activity on his daughter’s accounts since she vanished in May. NBC affiliate WGEM has been following Lindsey’s case since the first week of her disappearance, covering an early prayer vigil and the beginning of the investigation. Ten days after Lindsey vanished, the station spoke with Edina Mayor Linda Kerr. “I think the community is on edge, they’re wanting answers,” Kerr told WGEM. The Edina Sentinel has also reported extensively on the case. Knox County Sheriff Knoche told the newspaper that investigators had identified “people of interest” in the case but did not identify them by name. “The integrity of the investigation is my priority,” Knoche said. “Information to the public will be released at the appropriate time.” In mid-July, the Edina Sentinel and WGEM reported that investigators had executed multiple search warrants in Lindsey’s case. According to the documents, investigators searched a 2013 Ford F-150 and a black iPhone recovered from the vehicle. They also sought records from multiple cellphone providers and social media accounts. “The records do not accuse anyone of a crime or establish criminal wrongdoing,” the Sentinel wrote. “Instead, they show investigators seeking digital evidence they believed could help determine what happened after Watts was last seen on May 19.” At the 100-day mark of the investigation, Sheriff Knoche did a sit-down interview with the Edina Sentinel about the case. “We got the best team on it that we can,” he said. “The public just needs to be patient and trust in the process.” During the interview, Knoche said he believes foul play was involved in Lindsey’s disappearance. The sheriff said investigators had received hundreds of tips and he encouraged the public to call in with any information about Lindsey’s case. “My focus is on Lindsey Watts and finding her and bringing her home and ultimately bringing the individual or individuals involved in her disappearance to justice in a court of law,” Knoche told the Edina Sentinel. As the months pass without answers, Lindsey’s family is growing increasingly frustrated and fears the worst. “It’s coming to the point where we no longer believe she’s Earth-side,” sister Lacey told Dateline. With deer hunting season approaching, Lindsey’s family hopes hunters searching the wooded areas around Edina might come across something that could help locate her. “There’s a lot of out-of-state deer hunters up here,” John explained. The family is asking hunters to keep an eye out for any sign of Lindsey while they’re in the area. The Watts family is offering a $20,000 reward in Lindsey’s case to anyone who can tell the sheriff’s office “the whereabouts or the location of where she’s at, dead or alive,” John told Dateline. “We want her found.” Lacey echoed her father’s plea. “There’s really nothing left to say besides: Where is she at?” she said. Lindsey is around 5’3” and weighs approximately 125 lbs. She has long brown hair, brown eyes, and a tattoo of three stars on her right shoulder. If you have information about Lindsey’s case, please contact the Knox County Sheriff’s Office at 660-397-2186. If you have a story to share with Dateline, please submit it here.

articles.title: Zohran Mamdani has the most famous mustache in politics — for now
articles.summary: The New York City mayor swapped his familiar beard in favor of a Movember-inspired stache.
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani knows the power of maintaining a signature look in politics. When he began his campaign for the city’s top job, he swapped the South Asian collarless tunics, or kurtas, he’d gravitated to in his earlier career in favor of slender-cut suits that helped to balance his platform of democratic socialism with an air of the establishment. Those suits, and his trimmed beard, have remained key features of his style — so much so that it was not uncommon to see many men adopting the look as Halloween costumes this year. (Often with a New York Knicks jersey, to boot.) So it was something of a shock to see the mayor emerge over the weekend trying something new: a Mamdani mustache. While handing out water to runners at the New York City Marathon on Sunday, the mayor debuted his new facial hair, shaving his beard off to leave a standalone row of thick black hair above his upper lip. (Evidently, the look was so novel many runners raced past without recognizing him.) The mayor’s new look made instant headlines. New York magazine’s The Cut dubbed him “Mayor Mustache,” while the New York Post compared “the socialist’s shaving shake-up” to a “random redistribution of facial hair.” Others online debated whether Mamdani was more of a “beard guy.” Thanks to celebrities like Pedro Pascal and Benson Boone, mustaches have enjoyed something of a cultural renaissance in recent years, but it’s still a relatively rare look in politics. While certain foreign leaders have embraced the style (think ousted Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro or Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan), American male politicians tend to favor either a clean-shaven look or beard. For years, the most famous mustachioed figure in DC was John Bolton, whose rounded facial hair leaned more walrus than Wario. So was the mayor simply hopping on the mustache movement? Or was he trying to make a silent appeal to New York’s Italian or gay communities, where mustaches have long carried cultural cachet? The answer, it turns out, lies in men’s health. In a video posted to social media on Monday evening, the mayor revealed his mustache was in honor of Movember, the annual event in support of men’s health issues, such as prostate or testicular cancer. (Purists will say the mayor should have shaved all his facial hair off and grown a new one in from scratch, but we don’t begrudge Mamdani for wanting to avoid the awkward early days of wispy hair. Just ask Timothée Chalamet!) Twirling the ends of his new stache, the mayor said he wasn’t just paying “lip service” to the issues, highlighting a $4-million investment in a new prostate cancer center at a Brooklyn hospital. In addition to raising both funds and awareness, the Movember campaign, which began in Australia in 2003, also allows men like Mamdani to experiment with a mustache for a month before deciding whether to ditch it when December rolls around. So it remains to be seen whether Mamdani’s mo will stick around. Although one thing seems likely: he’s unlikely to grow it into a longer handlebar mustache. “What do you think?” he asked Council Member Rita C. Joseph, who appeared with him in the video. “Handlebar next?” “No, you’re going too far,” she replied.

articles.title: ‘We will find you, hunt you down’: Trump’s DHS secretary warns illegal voters on Election Day; Newsom fights it out with ICE
articles.summary: US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has issued a stern warning to people attempting to vote illegally in the United States, threatening that
articles.body: US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has issued a stern warning to people attempting to vote illegally in the United States, threatening that federal authorities will track them down and prosecute them as Americans head to polling stations for the November 3 midterm elections.“If you vote illegally in this country, and you are NOT eligible to vote, @DHSgov will find you, hunt you down, and you will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law. Only American citizens should be deciding American elections,” Mullin wrote in a post on X.The warning came on Election Day as voters across the country cast ballots in elections that will determine control of the US House of Representatives and Senate for the remaining two years of President Donald Trump's term.The same warning was echoed by the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement as ICE said: "If you vote illegally, we will find you. We will track you down, arrest you, and prosecute you. There will be no escape." California Governor Gavin Newsom issued a counter-warning to ICE and said: "If YOU show up to the polls illegally, we will find you. We will track you down, arrest you, and prosecute you. There will be no escape"Trump administration's crackdown on noncitizen votingThe Department of Homeland Security has been working to identify people it suspects of being noncitizens on state voter registration rolls. In July, Mullin sent letters to election officials in California, New Jersey, Nevada and Pennsylvania, claiming that preliminary reviews had identified more than 250,000 potential noncitizens registered to vote across the four states.According to DHS, the figures included 190,832 potential noncitizens in California, 35,152 in New Jersey, 15,903 in Nevada and 14,576 in Pennsylvania.However, the figures were disputed by election officials. Nevada Secretary of State Francisco Aguilar said the state's election office had not received supporting evidence for the department's claims and described the numbers as speculative.Pennsylvania Secretary of State Al Schmidt also said noncitizen voting was extremely rare and that the state would examine the information provided by DHS to evaluate its validity.The Trump administration has also expanded the use of the federal Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) programme to check citizenship information against voter registration records.Court blocks administration's latest election pushMullin's warning came amid legal challenges to the administration's efforts to identify suspected noncitizens on voter rolls.On November 3, a federal judge temporarily blocked the Justice Department and DHS from sending states lists of voters suspected of being noncitizens or encouraging officials to segregate or withhold their ballots until their citizenship was verified.US District Judge Tanya Chutkan expressed concerns about the reliability of the government's data and the possibility that eligible voters could be disenfranchised.Voting rights organisations and privacy groups have challenged the administration's efforts, arguing that the federal government is intruding into state election administration and relying on potentially inaccurate information.The administration has maintained that the measures are intended to enforce federal laws prohibiting noncitizens from voting.Can non-US citizens vote in American elections?Federal law prohibits non-US citizens from voting in federal elections, including elections for president and Congress. Violations can carry criminal penalties. Green Card holders can not vote.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: NTSB finds 'no evidence' of Mar-a-Lago connection after Florida jet crash kills nine people
articles.summary: The Learjet 60's left elevator was found miles from the Palm Beach County crash site, adding to evidence the jet broke apart before killing all nine aboard.
articles.body: A critical piece of the private jet that plunged into a Florida neighborhood was found miles from the impact site, federal investigators revealed Tuesday as crews prepared to drain the crater left by the crash that killed nine people. Asked about the crash occurring less than 10 miles from President Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago home and any potential connection to Secret Service operations, National Transportation Safety Board member Tom Chapman dismissed a link. "There is no evidence of connection. Purely coincidence," he said. FORMER NFL STAR SAYS HE PREVIOUSLY FLEW ON PRIVATE JET THAT CRASHED IN FLORIDA: 'ABSOLUTELY DEVASTATED' Most of the jet’s left elevator, a movable part of the tail that helps control the aircraft’s nose up or down, was recovered between 1.3 and 3.8 miles from the crash site, Chapman said. The discovery adds to evidence that the aircraft began breaking apart before impact. The elevator is a movable surface on the aircraft’s tail that helps control whether its nose points up or down. TEXAS FAMILY OF 4, 20-YEAR-OLD COPILOT AMONG 9 KILLED IN FIERY FLORIDA JET CRASH But Chapman said he did not believe the component would have enabled the aircraft to recover even if it had remained attached, given the speed of the jet’s descent. The Learjet was carrying seven passengers and two crew members from Austin, Texas, to North Eleuthera in the Bahamas when it crashed Sunday, killing everyone aboard. FAA SEEKS PERMANENT AIRSPACE RESTRICTIONS NEAR TRUMP’S MAR-A-LAGO AS EXPERT WARNS RULES ARE ‘NOT GOOD ENOUGH’ Investigators are now preparing to remove water from the impact crater, where Chapman said they expect to recover additional aircraft components. Given the force of the crash, pieces buried there will likely be small. Severe weather has hampered some recovery efforts, and weather remains a key focus of the investigation. The cause of the crash has not been determined. FAA, NTSB INVESTIGATING POSSIBLE VIOLATION OF SAFETY PROTOCOL INVOLVING TRUMP, MARINE ONE Investigators have also obtained dashcam footage to help reconstruct the aircraft’s final moments, Chapman said. Recovered wreckage is being retained for analysis, and officials urged anyone who encounters debris to leave it untouched and notify authorities. The crew had reported light clear ice and moderate turbulence while flying at about 35,000 feet before requesting permission to climb to 37,000 feet. Less than 30 seconds after controllers approved the request, the crew reported they were descending and issued a mayday call. Roughly 600 residents near Military Trail and Cresthaven Boulevard were evacuated after the crash, according to The Palm Beach Post. Between 40 and 50 people were staying at the Greenacres Community Center, Palm Beach County spokesperson John Jamason told the outlet. County officials were seeking state funding to help displaced residents with housing and transportation while authorities worked at the crash site. TRUMP HELICOPTER’S RADIO WARNINGS WENT UNHEARD BEFORE CLOSE CALL WITH PASSENGER JET, REPORT SAYS Officials said during Tuesday’s briefing that Military Trail remained closed in both directions between 10th Avenue North and Purdy Lane. They did not provide a timeline for reopening the road or allowing displaced residents to return home. Among those killed were Austin technology entrepreneur Adam Robinson, 45, his wife, Helen Sharp, 40, and their children, Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2. NORAD FIGHTER JETS INTERCEPT 2 AIRCRAFT NEAR TRUMP’S GOLF CLUB, 3RD PLANE DELAYS HIS NJ DEPARTURE Robinson, CEO and co-founder of Retention.com, had celebrated a business milestone in his final LinkedIn post the day of the crash, announcing that RB2B had reached $10 million in annual recurring revenue. He was also preparing for a live business debate scheduled for Tuesday. "Adam and Helen were devoted parents, and Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2, were the light of their lives. Helen and Adam were the love affair that will last forever," the families said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital. "Their warmth, generosity and gift for making people feel welcome touched so many lives. Their loss will be felt deeply by all those who loved them and who they loved in return." Chapman expressed confidence that investigators would determine what happened and thanked Florida and Palm Beach County authorities and first responders for their assistance. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Officials added that further investigative updates will be posted on the NTSB’s website. Fox News Digital's Greg Wehner contributed to this report.

articles.title: Texans vote in most expensive Senate race in US history
articles.summary: Pivotal Texas race for US Senate breaks spending records, with $573.2m poured into Paxton and Talarico campaigns.
articles.body:
Houston, Texas, the US – Texas voters have begun casting ballots in a consequential US Senate race that has already become the most expensive in United States history.

All told, at least $573.2m had been poured into support for both Republican candidate Ken Paxton and Democratic candidate James Talarico ahead of the Tuesday, November 3 vote.

The figure has included at least $212m to support Paxton from billionaire Elon Musk, whose SpaceX company is based in southern Texas .

The sum made voters of varying political persuasions queasy as they cast their ballots in a race that has been defined by affordability issues.

“That kind of money is being spent on the wrong stuff,” said Rico Sanchez, a 40-year-old union sheet metal worker who voted for Democrats based on the sky-high cost of living.

Kasey Blanco, a 21-year-old who split his ballot, voting for Republican Governor Greg Abbott and Democratic US Senate candidate Talarico, echoed the sentiment.

“It’s kind of scary,” he said. “You see the extent that a lot of these politicians are trying to get into the game and distort the view.”

Political power “should be from the people, by the people”, Blanco said.

The record spending has included both funds raised by the campaigns, as well as outside spending.

Talarico has outpaced Paxton in campaign funding, raising $155m to Paxton’s $40m. Federal law limits fundraising from individual donors, who must identify themselves.

Separately, a huge amount of money has poured in via political action committees called super PACs, which can spend an unlimited amount in support of a candidate but cannot directly coordinate with campaigns.

Paxton has been the largest beneficiary of such spending, including $168m from Musk to the Senate Leadership Fund, which has gone almost completely to supporting the Republican candidate, according to a New York Times analysis.

The newspaper estimated that Musk, who briefly and controversially led US President Donald Trump’s federal cost-cutting panel, the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), had spent at least $212m on Paxton, noting it was likely an undercount due to so-called “dark money” spending. Trump’s MAGA Inc PAC has spent at least $10m to support Paxton.

The Lone Star Rising PAC, meanwhile, has spent at least $21m on Talarico.

With national eyes on Texas, both US Senate candidates gave their closing pitches late Monday.

Talarico seized on Paxton’s past corruption allegations as Texas attorney general, drawing attention to Musk’s spending spree as evidence of prioritising big money interests over everyday voters.

His campaign has regularly referenced the “Friday Night Lights” television show, the story of an underdog American football team.

A Talarico victory would represent the first time a Democrat has won statewide office in Texas since 1994, with the party long hoping to “turn Texas blue”.

“We’re going to do something extraordinary,” Talarico said from San Antonio. “We’re going to do something historic. We’re going to shock the billionaires, shock the world, when we take back Texas.”

Paxton has portrayed Talarico as antithetical to the ideals of Texas, which has been dominated by Republicans for three decades. The state’s low-tax, low-regulation model, mixed with conservative social policies, has long given it special significance in Republican mythos.

Paxton’s campaign has repeatedly referenced the 1836 Texas Revolution, an uprising against then-Mexican control.

“We’ve never been this close to losing everything that we hold dear – our jobs, our livelihoods, our way of life in Texas,” he said at an event in Collin County. “If Texas falls, we don’t have another Texas to move to.”

Casting her ballot on Tuesday, 46-year-old Texas voter Monique Orellana said she was uncomfortable with Musk’s spending.

“He’s pouring all that money out here, trying to get whatever he’s trying to get,” she told Al Jazeera.

Regardless of party, she wanted elected officials to do their job and represent the people.

“I would vote for Republicans if I felt they were gonna do what they said they were gonna do. Right now I’m not feeling it,” she said.

“Trump said he wasn’t going to start a war, and he did anyway. And he said he was going to fix the price of groceries on day one. They went up anyway,” she said.

Voter Luis Plazas, 58, said he was not as concerned about the election spending, but wanted to see the economy improve and a pivot on Trump’s mass deportation campaign.

Still, he said, he voted Republican down the ballot, a decision he said was motivated by his religious beliefs.

“I’m a Christian, so I believe in family values, and it seems like Republicans are more inclined to that,” he said.

“I’m not really happy with the contenders or who I voted for, but my main concern right now is conservative values.”

articles.title: NTSB says crucial plane control parts found three miles from Florida crash site
articles.summary: The NTSB said because the parts were found far from the accident site, they fell off before the crash.
articles.body:
Crucial components of a private jet that crashed in Palm Beach, Florida - including a part that controlled the up-and-down movements of the nose of the plane - were found 1.3 (2 km) to 3.8 miles away from the crash site, an investigator said on Tuesday.

National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigators said they believed parts of the jet may have broken off before the Sunday crash, which killed all nine on board.

The NTSB found "the majority" of the Learjet's left elevator - a control surface on the tail - in three pieces, NTSB board member Tom Chapman said.

Chapman said because the parts were "quite some distance away" from the site, investigators determined they fell off before impact.

"Knowing that it was lost is a very important piece of evidence in terms of pointing us towards other things to investigate," he said.

Chapman said officials were still working out whether losing the left elevator caused the plane to nosedive or whether the part fell off because "forces on the aircraft caused that to separate".

He said the part of the plane that controls upward and downward movement may not have been "effective" at the speed the plane was travelling.

The Learjet 60 was bound for the Bahamas from Austin, Texas, when it nosedived into a multi-lane highway and exploded on impact.

In air traffic control audio recordings, someone in the cockpit can be heard reporting "moderate turbulence" and that the crew was "managing the ice".

They are then heard saying the plane was "picking up precipitation" and "we need to climb". Moments later, the same voice said the plane was descending at a rate of 10,000ft (3,048m) per minute.

An emergency was declared and the pilots can be heard yelling "we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute", before saying, "we are going to crash into the ground".

NTSB plans to investigate the role weather played in the crash. Officials were struggling to access the wreckage due to the huge crater created by the jet on a road in Palm Beach.

Chapman said on Tuesday that the force of the impact severely damaged the wreckage.

Seven passengers died on board, named in a joint statement as tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife, Helen Sharp, and their two children - Emma, four, and Charlie, two - as well as friends of the family Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, and Anita Maria Cetina, a nanny.

The pilot was named in media reports as 55-year-old Jeffrey Gregory. Nathalia Filgueiras, 20, who earned her pilot's licence when she was 17, was reported to be the co-pilot.

articles.title: Two helicopters collide near Mount Everest during rescue flight, killing one, injuring others
articles.summary: A tourist died after two helicopters collided near Pheriche below Mount Everest base camp. A 47-year-old man who was killed was from Chennai, India.
articles.body: Two helicopters collided while attempting to land just below Mount Everest base camp in Nepal. The accident happened at about 8:12 a.m. Tuesday in the Pheriche area of Solukhumbu District, according to a translated press release from the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal (CAAN). The helicopters were identified as an Air Dynasty aircraft and a Fishtail Air aircraft, the aviation authority said. Two foreign tourists were aboard the Fishtail Air helicopter. One of them, 47-year-old Vasanth Kumar Balaramudu of Chennai, India, died in the accident, according to CAAN. DEADLY HELICOPTER CRASH KILLS 2 PILOTS BATTLING RAGING WILDFIRE IN YOSEMITE The other tourist, New Zealand national Shailesh Kisan Patel, was injured, along with at least one pilot involved in the collision, the authority said. Those injured in the collision were admitted to a hospital in Kathmandu for further treatment, according to the aviation authority. CAAN has opened an investigation into the accident and will determine whether corrective action is needed based on its findings. Fishtail Air said its helicopter crashed during landing while transporting passengers rescued from the Everest region, Reuters reported. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The Air Dynasty helicopter was carrying only cargo, an official with the company told Reuters. Helicopters are a key form of transportation around Everest, where there are no roads. They are used to evacuate trekkers and guides suffering from illness or exhaustion amid the region's cold temperatures and high altitude, according to The Associated Press (AP). Pheriche, where the accident occurred, sits about 13,780 feet above sea level and is located below Everest base camp, the AP reported. The collision also came after heavy snow had covered trekking routes in the region. Conditions improved Sunday, allowing thousands of trekkers to begin moving through the area again, according to the outlet. In September, about 70 Americans remained unaccounted for following catastrophic flooding along the Nepal-China border, while 18 Americans had been confirmed safe, Fox News Digital previously reported. The flooding was triggered by an Aug. 26 glacier collapse and caused widespread destruction, including flash floods and landslides. Rescue crews were searching areas, including hydropower project tunnels, where workers were believed to be trapped. At least 1,399 people across Nepal and China's Tibet region died in the disaster, with more than 5,400 others still missing at the time of the report. articles.title: WATCH: Repeat offender leads deputies on 100 mph chase before hiding under porch in his underwear
articles.summary: Video captures Zakary Dean Hirschfield's 100 mph chase through Douglas County before deputies found him hiding beneath a porch in his underwear.
articles.body: A Colorado repeat offender turned a routine traffic stop into a dangerous chase and a manhunt that the district attorney says should never have happened. Zakary Dean Hirschfield, 24, of Centennial, received a five-year prison term after pleading guilty to felony eluding of a peace officer following the January pursuit through Douglas County, authorities said. Video released by the Douglas County Sheriff’s Office captures the nighttime escape, the pursuit through traffic and the moment deputies finally took Hirschfield into custody. REPEAT OFFENDER BUSTED AGAIN LESS THAN 24 HOURS AFTER RELEASE IN BRAZEN JEWELRY STORE THEFT CASE: POLICE District Attorney George Brauchler said Hirschfield should have been locked up before he ever hit the gas. "This case highlights the ripple effects of decisions made by other law enforcement agencies who had opportunities to lock this guy up before this dangerous episode," Brauchler said. The pursuit began when a Douglas County sheriff’s deputy pulled Hirschfield over for speeding in Castle Pines. During the stop, Hirschfield suddenly accelerated toward the deputy, forcing the deputy to jump out of the way to avoid being hit, authorities said. Video of the stop shows a deputy standing beside the vehicle before it abruptly pulls away. The deputy moves clear as the vehicle speeds down the residential street. FOUR WISCONSIN COPS INJURED AFTER SUSPECTED DRUNK DRIVER BARRELS TOWARD CROWD, SPARKS POLICE CHASE The deputy can be heard reporting over the radio that the driver tried to hit him. His female passenger screamed as he sped away, according to authorities. Hirschfield tore through Highlands Ranch and Littleton at speeds exceeding 100 mph, crossing medians and driving against traffic before crashing into another vehicle, according to authorities. SUSPECTED DUI DRIVER LEADS COPS ON WILD CHASE BEFORE DRAMATIC TAKEDOWN ON POPULAR CALIFORNIA BEACH Pursuit video shows deputies following the vehicle along roads busy with nighttime traffic, passing other motorists as emergency lights flash ahead. His passenger later told deputies she repeatedly begged him to stop. Instead, he abandoned her and the wrecked vehicle and ran, authorities said. WATCH: DEPUTIES HUNT WANTED MAN THROUGH CORNFIELD AFTER HIGH-SPEED CHASE CAUGHT ON CAMERA Dozens of deputies, specialized units and aerial resources joined the search, with drones and a K9 tracking Hirschfield through a Littleton neighborhood. Thermal drone video shows a person moving through an area with trees and brush as the aerial camera follows from above. COPPER THEFT SUSPECT'S DESPERATE ESCAPE CAUGHT ON BODYCAM VIDEO BEFORE DEPUTIES DISCOVER WHAT HE LEFT BEHIND About an hour after the initial traffic stop, deputies found Hirschfield beneath a porch, wearing only his underwear, authorities said. Body camera video shows deputies approaching a raised wooden structure with flashlights, then restraining the shirtless Hirschfield on the ground with his hands behind his back. "Put your hands behind your back, behind your back," a deputy orders as officers restrain him. A search of his vehicle turned up cocaine and drug paraphernalia, authorities said. "Don’t run from our deputies. We will catch you and hold you accountable," Douglas County Sheriff Darren Weekly said. "This defendant learned that the hard way and is now headed to prison. Putting our deputies and the public at risk will not be tolerated in Douglas County." The chase followed a series of earlier court decisions that Brauchler pointed to in criticizing Hirschfield’s repeated releases. FENTANYL DEATHS COULD NOW COST DRUG DEALERS THEIR LIVES UNDER NEW GOP PROPOSAL In November 2024, an Arapahoe County judge gave Hirschfield probation and community service after a plea agreement resulting in a conviction for attempted distribution of fentanyl, according to prosecutors. His probation was revoked less than three months later, but he was placed back on probation in June 2025. Another motion to revoke his probation was filed Aug. 19, 2025, the same day he was released without having to post cash bail in Jefferson County on a new felony robbery charge, prosecutors said. Five months later, he led deputies on the high-speed chase. "This defendant put countless lives at risk that evening," Deputy District Attorney Zach Idris said. "Thanks to the efforts of the Sheriff’s Office, Hirschfield will now spend several years in the Department of Corrections, where he will have plenty of time to think about his reckless actions that put him there." articles.title: Prince William says climate change makes UK wildfire risk terrifying
articles.summary: The prince says 2026 was the first summer he felt "worried about the scale of the wildfires".
articles.body:
There is a "terrifying prospect" of more UK wildfires in future due to climate change and preparation will be "crucial", the Prince of Wales has said.

Visiting Treherbert in Rhondda Cynon Taf, which was threatened by a huge mountain fire in August, Prince William praised a "gargantuan" effort to save homes, land and lives.

"We need to start taking wildfires as seriously as the continent has done," he said, raising issues such as a lack of firefighting aircraft.

He also suggested the community's response to the incident was an example for others to follow, after locals rallied around to support those fighting the flames.

The hillside, just metres away from the community centre where Prince William met fire crews, military personnel and local volunteers is burnt black.

"You looked up [and] the mountain was alight - it was like lava," explained Kath Edwards, managing director of charity Valleys Kids, which runs the building.

"I genuinely thought we were going to lose the centre - but more importantly people were going to lose their homes.

"You never think this is going to come literally to your door and that's what it was - it was just crazy."

South Wales Fire and Rescue Service (SWFRS) declared a major incident as it was forced to respond to 14 wildfires at the same time in August, including the one above Treherbert.

Support was drafted in from 22 other UK fire services while soldiers were deployed to dig fire breaks and help supply 2.1 million litres of water to douse the flames, including 200 members of the Queen's Own Gurkha Logistic Regiment.

Aled Bound, who is crew manager at Maesteg fire station and a retained - on-call - firefighter at Treorchy told Prince William it was "the hardest wildfire season" he and his colleagues had ever dealt with.

Months of record-breaking heat and dry conditions sparked a wave of wildfires across the UK through spring and summer.

He described it was "mentally and physically draining".

"I've never had to take so much water up a mountain to put on a fire and still come back the next day because that fire has relit, because it's so deep-seated," Bound said.

With climate change, he warned it "could well be a sign of what's to come".

Figures from the National Fire Chiefs Council show a new all-time high for recorded significant wildfires - 1,350 across England and Wales, up by more than 300 on 2025 and more than 1,000 on 2024.

Prince William told firefighters that 2026 was the first summer "where I've felt generally worried about the scale of the wildfires in the country".

He added: "We might go again next season... it's quite a terrifying prospect if we're not... on the ball."

He asked about availability of firefighting aircraft , noting that "the need for aerial assets has been hoisted quite high up in government" as an area "we're lacking".

He recalled flying water bowsers in the Falklands "putting out range fires... and once the Sea King went, we don't have the assets any more".

"I think it's front and centre of many people's minds now, how do we recreate that."

Conversation turned to the kit available to fire crews working in unbearable heat, proactive land management practices and whether social media firms could do more to discourage people from setting fires.

Recently, the UK government announced that the RAF's Chinook helicopters and A400M aircraft would be equipped to fight fires in future.

A separate Welsh government wildfire summit also led to promises of action to improve preparedness .

"It feels like this is something we're going to have to live with as a country or as a world now every summer," Prince William said.

"It's fair to say that we've learnt a lot from this season... and there's lots that we'll be putting into place, particularly following the wildfire summits," said Adam Openshaw, deputy chief fire officer for SWFRS.

He described the response of people in Treherbert as "the best demonstration of the community coming together to support the wildfire response".

He said it really helped as fire crews worked "tirelessly" in "challenging circumstances".

Edwards explained that volunteers kept the community centre open 24 hours a day from the Saturday evening of the fire until the following Thursday "to provide whatever service we could".

Due to the unprecedented nature of the fire, the centre became a control hub for the firefighting operation, a place to rest and regroup and a focal point for people wanting to show their support.

Businesses donated food - "40 pizzas arrived within the first 20 minutes" - and there were regular visits from an ice cream van.

Prince William asked whether volunteers should be used more in future and was told the community's efforts, hand in hand with military support, enabled the fire service to focus on bringing the incident under control.

"From something really quite horrific, the valleys did what the valleys do very, very well - we pulled together to make a difference," Edwards said.

Communities in the south Wales valleys were already experiencing the effects of climate change, she warned.

"We've had floods, fires... we've got [coal] tips that move as well.

"I think the message I was keen to get across is... we are motivated as a community to ask how do we solve this?

"How can we work together as a community and voluntary sector to support agencies [like the fire service]?"
