articles.title: Denholm ecologist battles for custody of badger he rescued
articles.summary: Graeme Wilson says Harriet the badger would be hurt or killed if she was released back into the wild.
articles.body:
An ecologist in the Scottish Borders is fighting to be allowed to keep a badger that he saved from starvation.

Graeme Wilson was called out to help the cub, called Harriet, in April after she was found in a cattle trough 100m (300ft) from her sett.

Wilson nursed the badger back to health but believes she was hand-reared prior to being picked her up and it would be impossible to return her to the wild.

NatureScot - which turned down his application for an educational licence to keep the animal - said it was continuing talks to try to find a "pragmatic solution".

Wilson runs GW Ecology, a small independent rescue and rehabilitation service at his home in Denholm.

It carries out surveys to determine whether protected species are present on the sites of proposed property developments.

He also leads bat walks, workshops and holds educational events about wildlife and how to protect it.

Wilson describes himself as an "experienced and trained wildlife rehabber" who has cared for a variety of wildlife over the years.

He argues that an educational licence could allow him to support public understanding of badgers, wildlife rescue and caring for a protected species.

He said that after rescuing Harriet, it quickly became evident to him that she could not go back to where he found her.

Wilson added: "It was almost second nature when she saw the bottle.

"I have cared for injured badgers before and never have I seen something like it.

"It was clear then she couldn't be released back into the wild."

He said NatureScot, the public body responsible for Scotland's natural heritage and wildlife, had told him she should be returned to the wild or sent to a zoo.

However, he believes that releasing Harriet into the wild would only result in her being hurt or killed.

He said: "Badgers are companion animals, they are a social animal and unfortunately for Harriet she has decided that humans are her social group.

"Can you imagine Harriet approaching someone on a dog walk or in the street?

He said a zoo would also be unsuitable for Harriet, arguing she would become lonely and suffer unnecessary distress.

"Harriet's upbringing means she needs human interaction, not to be put behind glass and stared at," he said.

Wilson said he would keeping fighting to hold on to Harriet.

However, he admitted there may not be a lot he can do, despite having the support of several badger rescue groups in Scotland.

Police Scotland has been made aware of the situation.

NatureScot said talks were ongoing to try to find a way to resolve the issue.

"We are continuing discussions with Mr Wilson and other relevant organisations to try and find a pragmatic solution to this individual situation," said a spokesperson.

"The welfare of the badger is, of course, key while we consider the circumstances of the case."

Scottish SPCA advice is that any badger cub discovered outside its sett before it is about 12 weeks old - or about the size of a domestic cat - is likely to need help.

It said any member of the public coming across a sick or injured badger should not attempt to hold or touch the animal until one of its rescue officers arrives.

"Badgers can become aggressive if they are in pain or feel threatened; they can give a nasty bite and their sharp claws could cause serious injury, if you try to catch it," it said.

"You should also contact us if you find a badger during daylight hours as they may be struggling."

articles.title: Greene says Trump’s Israel aid announcement shows ‘how bad the polling is’
articles.summary: Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.) on Tuesday said that President Trump’s recent announcement about cutting aid to Israel shows “how bad the polling is” when it comes to the issue. “Trump getting permission from Netanyahu to end annual aid to Israel isn’t going to change today’s election results,” Greene said in a Tuesday morning…
articles.body:
Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.) on Tuesday said that President Trump’s recent announcement about cutting aid to Israel shows “how bad the polling is” when it comes to the issue.

“Trump getting permission from Netanyahu to end annual aid to Israel isn’t going to change today’s election results,” Greene said in a Tuesday morning post on the social platform X.

“Nor is it going to end the war with Iran or stop Israel from murdering innocent Palestinians. But it does show you how bad the polling is on that issue,” the former Georgia lawmaker added.

On Tuesday, Trump said that he had come to a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that will stop U.S. aid to Israel this year.

In an interview on Fox News’s “Fox & Friends,” Trump said that he and the Israeli leader made a deal “months ago” for the U.S. to cut off its aid to Israel.

“They’re fine with it,” the president said. “They’ve become a very successful country. They don’t need it, and we won’t be paying anymore.”

The issue of American aid to Israel has become more prominent in the last few years, especially in the wake of Israel’s war in Gaza. Many have accused Israel of “genocide” with its actions in Gaza, with tens of thousands of Palestinians dead in the territory due to the conflict.

“Last year when my amendment to strip funding to Israel failed in the House bc only 6 members of congress including myself voted for it, I was labeled an antisemite,” Greene said in her Tuesday post. “Amazing how being on the verge of Republicans getting wiped out in the midterms changes hearts and minds.”

Earlier this year , Greene resigned from Congress amid a feud with Trump. She had criticized Trump’s handling of files linked to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and a perceived lack of attention from the president on lowering costs.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.
